title: Western Brands Need a New China Playbook
subtitle: After an almost three-year slump, China’s luxury market is showing signs of recovery. Western brands need to act quickly by rationalizing distribution, localizing output, and planning for the future to increase relevance.
author: Joe Bobowicz
hero_image_alt: Western Brands Need a New China Playbook
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Joe Bobowicz.
content:
Western luxury in China has hit serious roadblocks in recent years. The old approach of opening stores and investing in top-down marketing is now ineffective, as local consumers look elsewhere for authenticity and clear value propositions. And so, the brands that rise to the challenge by localizing their output, optimizing distribution, and adapting to China’s new consumer will be best placed when the market recovers.

“I think the relationship between Chinese consumers and Western brands is undergoing a significant shift,” says Cherry Xu, founder of Shanghai-based fashion-art foundation Cheruby. “Younger generations no longer automatically associate Western origins or heritage with greater value.”

The latest round of earnings revealed that China’s luxury market is taking longer to stabilize than hoped. According to Bain’s report released early this year, the mainland Chinese personal luxury market contracted 3-5% in 2025. And although it displayed signs of recovery in the second half of the year, fashion, specifically, is still struggling. “There have been quite a few [Chinese] store closures, and I think the mood is unsupportive of luxury,” Goldman Sachs luxury analyst Erwan Rambourg told Vogue Business in October.

“The third quarter brought a more challenging Chinese consumer backdrop with a ‘feel-good’ factor deteriorating at the very beginning of the quarter,” LVMH CFO Cécile Cabanis said during the group’s earnings call in October. Until June, Hermès was growing in Greater China, but is now broadly flat year-on-year following the Q3 results due to a decline in traffic. Kering declined 8% in the Asia-Pacific region, excluding Japan. CEO Luca de Meo said in a statement that “delivering our action plan in China” will help the group to restore momentum. At Prada Group , too, China remained a weak point.

“Weaker consumer confidence, slower economic growth, and heightened price sensitivity are weighing on discretionary spending, following more than a decade in which China was a key driver of global luxury growth,” said Fflur Roberts, head of luxury goods at Euromonitor International.

In recent years, domestic brands have shone in China by embracing their native understanding of Chinese cultural sensibilities and offering better value for money, as consumers show heightened price sensitivity — a big drag on the discretionary spending that once drove major growth for global luxury players. Local brands are especially well placed to adapt to the rising “Guochao” (direct translation: “national tide”) movement, which incorporates traditional Chinese style elements into contemporary styles.

Chinese luxury consumers continue to engage with Chanel, despite a sluggish market. Pictured: Shan Yichun.

Additionally, Western luxury brands must increasingly compete with a shift in China’s premium consumption. China International Capital Corporation’s (CICC) vice president Liwei Hou reports that overall tenant sales at Chinese high-end malls outperformed luxury brand growth in 2025 and 2026. “Sportswear (Arc’teryx, Salomon) and affordable brands (like Ralph Lauren), as well as Chinese brands (Laopu, Songmont), and fine dining have been the star performers in these high-end malls,” she says. “A crisis of luxury is an opportunity for others. Proactive changes are needed.”

Until Western brands audit their approach — a time-consuming and complex process — domestic Chinese brands may continue to capture market share, analysts agree, capitalizing on the cost-effective manufacturing infrastructure at their fingertips, which makes room for bigger margins.

For starters, Western brands must adapt to the leading consumer. Experts agree that the commercial backbone for luxury brands in China is the established millennial and Gen X clients, particularly for bigger-ticket purchases.

In Bain’s 2025 report on China’s personal luxury goods market, the firm found that consumer motivations for buying luxury had shifted away from signaling status to a more refined appreciation and discernment. “The Chinese consumer hasn’t stopped spending. They’ve stopped overpaying for a logo. Status has moved from visible wealth to taste, craft, and wellbeing,” says Jonathan Travers-Smith, CEO of Hotpot, an agency bringing Western brands into East Asian markets. Brands must demonstrate real craft, a credible story and prices that feel earned, Travers-Smith advises. “Some Western houses have priced their way out of that conversation, raising prices year after year while the in-store experience stayed the same.” In addition, he argues, brands should halt price hikes and invest in clienteling.

“The industry has spent a lot of time talking about creativity and marketing, but I think the bigger challenge is rebuilding a sense of value,” says Thomas Chauvet, Citi’s head of luxury goods research. Simply lowering prices is not the answer, he believes. Rather, brands must develop stronger products, better assortments, greater differentiation, and a clearer reason for consumers to buy.

Burberry’s approach to China is working well , confirmed CEO Joshua Schulman on the investor call earlier this month. Greater China’s retail growth grew (5%) in Q2 of fiscal 2026, carried by local spending. This followed a 9% climb in Q1. “We clearly understand that the market in China is challenging right now,” said Schulman. “That said, we are pleased with our outperformance in a dynamic market. And this has been going on for several quarters.” The brand, he revealed, had risen to the challenge over the last two years, aligning pricing with consumer expectations — aware that globally, and in China especially, consumers were fatigued by exorbitant price points. “This was a historic positioning that we had,” said Schulman. “And coming back to this sweet spot in the luxury market has been a priority for us. We see that this is resonating strongly with our Chinese consumers.”

The Western brands that are performing have renewed desire through fresh ideas, centered on experiences, travel, beauty and wellness, not just novelty for novelty’s sake. “Creative leadership is central to this process. Matthieu Blazy’s appointment at Chanel offers an example of how a new creative direction can introduce a fresh perspective to an established house and generate renewed consumer interest,” says Julio Ng, co-founder of brand development consultancy 2034. It’s understood that Chanel is performing well in China , despite the downturn for other players.

Ralph Lauren is another outlier. Brand CEO Patrice Louvet told investors earlier this month that China sales remained strong in Q2, increasing more than 35%, bolstered by store sales as well as distribution expansion. Its output remains rooted in premium American style that’s more affordable than most luxury players, resonating with value-conscious Chinese consumers.

“What Chanel and Ralph Lauren do particularly well is that they both have a very distinct sense of world-building,” says Xu. “Chanel has established a cultural presence beyond fashion through art, cinema, and creative expression, while Ralph Lauren offers an entire lifestyle and aesthetic universe.” She argues that both remain true to their identities while creating different entry points into their worlds, noting that brands wanting to build lasting brand value need a clear identity, compelling products, and a consistent creative vision.

Ralph Lauren grew China sales more than 35% in the last quarter. Pictured: Actor Kevin Chu.

Calvin Wang, a luxury and retail consultant, is dubbing it the shift to “rational indulgence”. He explains that VICs should be respected as connoisseurs. “Approach clients with the understanding that they often know more and have seen more than the brand’s frontline staff,” he says. Wang encourages a focus on UHNWIs to handle the K-shaped economy, where the top end of the economy grows, but the lower end lags as inequalities widen. However, he still recommends maintaining connections to upper-middle-class consumers by offering products of demonstrable quality and longevity.

“When it comes to what brands can control, I think that the focus has to be on reigniting product desirability, so investing in marketing and in innovative retail experience should be the priority,” says Carole Madjo, luxury goods analyst at Barclays.

In the past, international brands have struggled to land a successful localization strategy in China, often oversimplifying the process. “A China strategy cannot simply be an adaptation of global marketing materials,” says Olivia Chen, co-founder of Shanghai-based brand agency 2034. “Local teams need sufficient understanding of the brand, as well as the authority to make decisions that respond to the market. At the same time, local activity needs to remain aligned with the brand’s international positioning.” Chen sees it as a balancing act. If a Western brand becomes too localized, it loses the qualities that first made it attractive — that is, what the brand represents beyond China.

“With the increasingly global circulation of information and culture, younger generations are developing their own sensibilities and identities at the intersection of global culture and local experience,” says Xu. “Rather than approaching Chinese consumers as a distinctly separate audience, brands are engaging with individuals who have both a global cultural perspective and their own local experiences. I think this is changing the way we understand localization.”

Burberry’s localization approach? “Combining our British luxury heritage with locally relevant product and storytelling,” said Schulman on the brand’s most recent investor call. “In the second quarter, we had capsule collections for Chinese Valentine’s Day, and we also had a localized activation with China National Geography. All of those show our appreciation for and understanding of the local customer.”

To this day, major brands still produce red-colored Lunar New Year collections. But they should “avoid superficial ‘Guochao’ tokenism,” warns Wang. “Designing literal Chinese-themed capsules — such as applying zodiac animals or traditional calligraphy onto Western silhouettes — frequently reads as opportunistic and patronizing. Chinese luxury consumers already look to domestic designers for authentic cultural expression.”

Equally, brands must develop strong strategies beyond local celebrity endorsements and seasonal campaigns. Travers-Smith takes a hardline on this. “Listen before you spend. Go deep into Xiaohongshu and Douyin for insights into how consumers actually talk about your category, your product, and competitors,” he says. “Build one or two cultural moments a year that are made in China — not adapted for China.” He also encourages empowering an on-the-ground China digital team to make decisions, embrace faster content cycles, and cater content based on different market needs across cities.

For a Western luxury house, Burberry is outperforming in the China market thanks to effective localization. Pictured: Actor Wu Lei.

Travers-Smith pinpoints a big misconception that Chinese social media is a channel for pushing campaigns. The reality? “It’s where consumers decide what to buy, and Xiaohongshu is a search engine for taste. Building beautifully polished brand-owned content should be the second priority after ensuring your brand is communicated through UGC from influencers and key opinion leaders (KOLs).”

As for product assortment and store networks, brands should streamline, Bismuth recommends. This means closing underperforming stores, moving away from promotional activity, and slowing down on retail expansion. This shift is already underway. Louis Vuitton, Dior, Loro Piana, and Tiffany opened new flagship stores in Tier-1 cities while scaling back presence in Tier-2 and Tier-3 locations over recent years. Nonetheless, some insiders favor a more selective approach over a blanket Tier-1-only strategy. One core takeaway experts agree on: treat China as a continent made up of several unique territories.

Western companies must also take stock of their wholesale and direct-to-consumer (DTC) networks. “Brands need people who understand their positioning and can represent them in a way that supports their long-term ambitions,” says Chen. “China is a complex market to navigate, and a brand’s reputation can be affected by how and where its products are sold.”

The Chinese DTC landscape is fundamentally different from the rest of the world’s. Discovery, communication, and client relationships are built predominantly on platforms like WeChat’s mini-programs (sub-applications often used for e-commerce) and Tmall Luxury Pavilion (a premium e-concession platform). “Brands must focus on connecting and aligning the distinct strengths of each platform to create a seamless consumer journey,” says Wang.

Because of the macro downturn and the growing maturity of a relatively new major market, analysts struggle to outline a recovery timeline for Western luxury in China. One thing is clear: brands should not wait it out. “The slump might be cyclical, but the change in behavior is structural,” says Travers-Smith. “Property wealth isn’t coming back to 2021 levels, and the consumer who learned to buy less and better isn’t going to unlearn it.”

The smartest players will address issues the boom hid and strategize for potential market disruptors. “For 2027, watch AI. Assistants like Doubao and Qwen are becoming the first place people ask what to buy,” warns Travers-Smith. “If your brand isn’t described accurately and favorably in those answers, you’re invisible at the moment of consideration.”

In the mid to long-term, luxury houses should also ramp up their knowledge and insights on Chinese Gen Z and Gen Alpha. “[They] are expected to become important pillars for businesses in 10-20 years, and it is never too early to start understanding them and interacting with them,” says Hou. Even today, the Gen Z contingent might not drive direct revenue, but they can give brands cultural relevance.

China’s Gen Z isn’t a core consumer yet, but Western brands should continue to court the group. Pictured: Actor Wang Yibo.

“I would love to see more brands move beyond cultural marketing and towards cultural production. This could mean building long-term relationships with local artists, designers, and independent cultural institutions, supporting research, commissioning new work, and encouraging cross-disciplinary exchanges,” says Xu. “These investments may take longer to develop, but they have the potential to create value for both the brand and the local cultural ecosystem.”

For Western brands, waiting it out is not a viable option. It’s an expensive mistake. Chauvet encourages action: “Chinese luxury demand may recover, but I suspect the market that emerges will be more mature and more competitive than the one brands enjoyed over the past decade.”

title: What the EU’s Plan to Abandon the Green Claims Directive Means for Fashion
subtitle: Anti-greenwashing rules still apply, but brands may be left without a common framework for substantiating environmental claims.
author: Jessica Binns
hero_image_alt: What the EU’s Plan to Abandon the Green Claims Directive Means for Fashion
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Jessica Binns.
content:
On November 4, the European Commission placed the proposed Green Claims Directive on a list of legislation it intends to withdraw within six months. The proposal would have set common rules for substantiating and independently verifying voluntary environmental claims. Its planned withdrawal comes just five weeks after separate anti- greenwashing rules began applying across the EU, leaving fashion brands with continued obligations and less direction on how claims should be proven.

The November listing confirms an intention the Commission first signaled in June 2025, prompting the Council to cancel a planned final round of negotiations. The proposal remains formally pending until the withdrawal process is completed, although its revival appears unlikely. The Commission says efforts to advance it during 2025 failed and that it is unlikely to secure sufficient support from member states within a reasonable timeframe.

If withdrawn, the directive’s prescribed substantiation and pre-publication verification process would never take effect, sparing companies some upfront costs. Existing obligations under the EU Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, or EmpCo, and broader consumer law would remain, leaving companies to interpret the rules and carry the legal risk.

EmpCo has already strengthened EU consumer law against greenwashing, including restrictions on unqualified claims such as “green” and “eco-friendly”, sustainability labels that lack a qualifying certification scheme or public authority behind them, and product claims of carbon neutrality based on offsetting. It also requires claims about future environmental performance to be supported by a detailed implementation plan with measurable targets and regular independent verification.

The Green Claims Directive would have gone further by prescribing how companies should substantiate explicit environmental claims — for example, that a garment has a lower carbon footprint or uses less water — and requiring independent verification before those claims reached consumers. Its withdrawal could leave brands with fewer mandatory steps but less certainty about the evidence regulators will expect.

For fashion, the question of proof travels upstream. Consumer-facing claims often depend on data from textile mills, garment factories and raw-materials suppliers; as brands develop their own evidence requirements, manufacturers serving several customers could face a sprawling patchwork of reporting demands.

Withdrawing the directive would eliminate a prescribed substantiation and verification process, along with some of its upfront costs. Companies would still need to assess their claims and supporting evidence under EmpCo and existing consumer law, placing more of the judgment and legal risk inside the business, leading to uncertainty.

That uncertainty is already being felt inside fashion companies. One sustainability executive at a fashion brand, speaking on background because they were not authorized to discuss the company’s regulatory preparations, says the rapid succession of EU rules has left substantial room for interpretation, making compliance difficult even for companies acting in good faith.

Though brands would avoid some of the initial costs associated with the proposed verification regime, they will still need to identify potentially risky claims, assess whether the underlying evidence supports them and decide when further substantiation, qualification or other safeguards are necessary. That analysis will happen claim by claim, with national regulators and courts interpreting the common EU rules as cases emerge.

The attorneys say companies should hold evidence that directly relates to the claim, remains current and can be independently verified. EmpCo provides clearer boundaries around prohibited practices, but it does not supply the comprehensive methodology that the Green Claims Directive was intended to establish.

That leaves room for differences among EU member states. EmpCo establishes a common EU legal baseline, and the attorneys expect national approaches to remain broadly similar. Member-state regulators and courts could still apply those rules differently to individual claims, particularly before further guidance and case law emerge.

The European Commission could reduce some of that uncertainty through guidance and coordination, but it cannot fully recreate the detailed, harmonized framework envisioned by the abandoned proposal, the attorneys add.

Consumer advocates are particularly concerned about the loss of pre-publication verification. EmpCo enables authorities to challenge prohibited or misleading claims after they enter the market. The Green Claims Directive would have required covered claims and labels to clear an independent check beforehand.

National enforcement authorities already face limited resources and an enormous volume of environmental marketing, say Blanca Morales, head of sustainable consumption and production at the European Consumer Organisation, known as BEUC, and Patrycja Gautier, its head of consumer rights and product safety.

Assessing the evidence behind a claim can require technical expertise and lengthy investigation. In the meantime, the marketing remains visible. Claims can circulate for years before authorities intervene, Morales and Gautier say, by which point “the harm is already done”.

The absence of a common methodology also makes comparison harder. Companies may use different calculations to describe the environmental footprint of clothing, leaving shoppers unable to assess products on equivalent terms. The problem is particularly acute in fashion, where retailers and platforms have introduced an array of proprietary sustainability scores, labels and filters, says BEUC.

The planned withdrawal could therefore reduce certainty for companies as well as consumers. EmpCo prohibits generic environmental claims unless a company can demonstrate recognized environmental performance and creates specific rules for labels, future targets and offset-based marketing. It provides less direction on the methodology companies should use to substantiate other explicit claims.

The enforcement picture could still evolve. On November 11, the Commission separately proposed changes to the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation that would allow it to investigate major cross-border infringements directly and impose fines of up to 6% of a company’s worldwide annual turnover. The proposal could strengthen enforcement against EU-wide greenwashing, but it must still pass through the legislative process.

Large fashion companies are unlikely to dismantle their sustainability systems because one proposed directive disappears.

“Our approach to sustainability is grounded in long-term commitments, not individual regulatory requirements,” says Jeff Hogue, head of global sustainability at Gap Inc. The company will continue complying with applicable rules and believes environmental claims should be “clear, credible and supported by evidence”, he adds. Gap also favors consistent standards across markets, which it says help companies communicate progress while maintaining consumer trust.

Those long-term programs still depend on information from suppliers. Brands will likely continue requesting data on materials, energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, driven by corporate sustainability strategies, investor expectations, public pressure and other regulatory mandates, says Dr. Sheng Lu, professor and director of graduate studies in fashion and apparel studies at the University of Delaware.

That dependence creates legal exposure across the supply chain. A brand can face scrutiny under consumer-protection and advertising laws if its environmental claim is misleading or inadequately substantiated, even when the underlying information came from a supplier, says Meaghan Colligan Hembree of DLA Piper. An upstream supplier may separately face exposure over representation made to the brand and its contractual obligations. How that risk is allocated will depend on the facts and the agreements between the parties.

With the Green Claims Directive’s proposed verification system unlikely to take effect, contracts and internal governance could carry greater weight. Hembree expects brands to scrutinize what suppliers are asked to represent, the substantiation accompanying that information, their audit and verification rights, how environmental data is updated and who bears responsibility for inaccuracies.

“From a litigation standpoint, that paper trail can become critically important in understanding who knew what, what the ultimate claim was based on, and where the information may have broken down,” she says.

Those requirements could vary by buyer. Large fashion companies already use their commercial leverage to determine which certifications, calculations and disclosures suppliers must provide, Lu says. Manufacturers serving several customers may then have to satisfy multiple standards and reporting systems, adding to the cost of collecting and sharing data.

The burden will be particularly difficult for smaller suppliers, brands and exporters to absorb. Smaller brands and exporters without dedicated European legal teams may struggle to adapt their claims and evidence across national markets. Suppliers face a different burden: meeting multiple buyers’ data requirements, often without the staff or systems to do so, Lu says.

Regulatory uncertainty could also shape sourcing decisions. Lu expects fashion companies to consolidate their supplier bases as they seek manufacturers with the infrastructure, data and trust needed to support environmental claims. Strategic supplier relationships will become more valuable when brands need reliable information extending from raw materials through production.

The early evidence may appear in product descriptions and sourcing questionnaires rather than corporate targets. Lu will be watching whether brands replace broad sustainability language with narrower, measurable claims, alongside changes in the data they require suppliers to provide.

Fashion companies should not wait for enforcement actions to establish the boundaries, the Loyens & Loeff attorneys say. They recommend reviewing environmental and social claims, checking whether sustainability labels meet the rules already in force, aligning language across consumer communications and creating processes to document and regularly reassess the supporting evidence.

“The framework may still develop, but the compliance obligation is already there,” the attorneys say, “and so are the risks of regulatory scrutiny, sanctions and civil litigation.”

title: Mario Sorrenti: The Life Behind the Images
subtitle: In Paris, an exhibition of Mario Sorrenti's personal diaries from the 1990s reveals the life, relationships and experiences behind some of fashion photography's most iconic images. An intimate journey into the world of a photographer who transformed the way we see beauty, desire and sensuality.
author: Alessia Glaviano
author_role: Global Head of Photovogue & Visual Director
hero_image_alt: Mario Sorrenti: The Life Behind the Images
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Alessia Glaviano.
content:
During Paris Photo, I visited Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000 , an exhibition curated by Aaron Stern at LSD, a small gallery on Rue de la Folie Méricourt, in a space that once housed a photographic laboratory. The room was packed, almost overwhelmingly so, and what struck me immediately was the number of young people there. A generation that has grown up with smartphones, accustomed to producing and consuming images at an unprecedented speed, seemed completely fascinated by these handmade books, filled with photographs, Polaroids, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of a life lived more than thirty years ago.

I found myself wondering what drew them so strongly to these objects. Was it nostalgia for a time they had never experienced? A fascination with the physicality of photography, with the idea that images once existed as tangible things, objects to be touched, collected, cut, pasted and preserved? Or perhaps something more profound: a longing for authenticity, for the traces of real experiences, for a relationship with images that feels increasingly distant from the way we encounter them today?

The more I looked at Mario's diaries, the more I felt that the answer lay somewhere in that last possibility.

Courtesy of Mario Sorrenti Diaries , LSD Paris

Mario Sorrenti is one of the defining photographers of his generation , an artist whose work has profoundly influenced the visual language of fashion photography since the early 1990s. His contribution to Vogue Italia alone is extraordinary. Over the years, he has created an extensive body of editorials that remain part of the magazine's visual history, images that helped shape not only the aesthetics of fashion but also the way fashion could communicate desire, intimacy and emotion.

His signature is unmistakable, yet it cannot be reduced to a particular technique or aesthetic formula. There is the extraordinary sensitivity with which he approaches light, whether soft and natural or dramatic and carefully controlled. There is his attention to skin, texture and the physical presence of the body, his ability to move between the immediacy of a seemingly spontaneous photograph and the formal sophistication of an elaborately constructed image.

Above all, there is his particular way of representing sensuality.

Fashion photography has always had a complex relationship with desire, and Mario certainly wasn't the first photographer to explore intimacy or eroticism. But he brought something distinctly his own to that tradition. In his photographs, sensuality never feels imposed on the subject. It seems to emerge from the relationship between the photographer and the person in front of his camera. Even when an image is provocative, there is often a tenderness, a vulnerability, an emotional proximity that prevents it from becoming merely an exercise in seduction.

Perhaps the most famous example remains his photographs of Kate Moss, who was his girlfriend at the time, particularly the images that led to the iconic Calvin Klein Obsession campaign in 1993. Their extraordinary power came not simply from Kate's beauty or Mario's photographic talent, but from the genuine intimacy of their relationship. These were not images in which intimacy was staged for the camera. They emerged from an existing emotional connection, from a shared life, before becoming part of the collective visual memory of an era.

And this is where the exhibition in Paris becomes especially revealing.Rather than presenting the celebrated photographs that established Mario's reputation, it turns its attention to the world from which those images emerged.

The five diaries, spanning the years between 1991 and 2000, bring together photographs, contact sheets, handwritten notes, drawings and fragments of everyday life . For the exhibition, Mario reproduced the pages of his original journals using color Xerox machines, then reassembled and bound them by hand. These are not conventional photographic books, nor simply archival documents. They occupy a fascinating territory between memory, artistic experimentation and the physical act of making.

There are portraits, faces, bodies, moments of everyday life, images of friends and lovers, familiar figures from the fashion world, and deeply personal traces of the people who surrounded him. There are handwritten words, repetitions, experiments, sequences of images that seem to follow the associative logic of memory rather than the conventions of photographic editing.

What makes this particularly fascinating is that Mario's diaries were not simply something he created alongside his photographic career. They were fundamental to its development. He began taking pictures in New York in the late 1980s, teaching himself photography while documenting the world around him, even building a darkroom in his mother's laundry room. It was precisely these personal diaries that, when he showed them to Calvin Klein in 1993, inspired the iconic Obsession campaign.

The boundary between personal work and commissioned photography was never as clear as we might imagine. For many great photographers, this distinction becomes almost meaningless. It is precisely their personal vision, shaped by experiences, relationships and an ongoing process of exploration, that makes their work immediately recognizable, regardless of the context in which it is created. At its highest level, fashion photography is no longer simply in the service of a product, but becomes a space for genuine artistic exploration.

The photographs are inseparable from the people Mario loved, the places he inhabited and the cultural atmosphere that shaped him. What emerges is not only the development of a photographic language but the formation of a sensibility.

I was particularly touched by this because I lived in New York during those same years. Mario and I belong to the same generation, and although our experiences were our own, we inhabited the same city, at the same moment, within a cultural world that was undergoing an extraordinary transformation.

New York in the 1990s was a place of intense creative exchange, where fashion, photography, music, art and nightlife constantly intersected. There was a sense of freedom, experimentation and possibility, but also a rawness, an urgency, a willingness to take risks and to blur the boundaries between one's personal life and creative work.

Looking through Mario's diaries, I recognized something of that world. Not necessarily the same people or the same experiences, but the atmosphere, the energy, the particular feeling of being young in a city where life and creativity seemed impossible to separate.

There is also the extraordinary family Mario comes from, a remarkable constellation of creative talent. His mother, Francesca Sorrenti, a woman of exceptional talent and an enormously influential figure in the worlds of fashion and image-making; his sister Vanina, an extraordinarily gifted photographer in her own right; and his younger brother Davide, who died tragically young in 1997, an exceptional photographer whose work captured the spirit of a generation with rare sensitivity and immediacy.

In this family, photography has never been simply a profession. It has been a shared language, a way of relating to one another and to the world. Perhaps this helps explain why Mario's work feels so deeply personal, even when it is created within the highly sophisticated machinery of the fashion industry.

Davide's presence in the diaries is particularly poignant. Knowing his story, these images become more than fragments of a shared youth. They are traces of a relationship, of love, of loss, of a world that no longer exists except through the images that remain.

And this brings us back to something fundamental about photography: its extraordinary relationship with time.

A photograph preserves a moment while simultaneously reminding us that the moment is gone. But in Mario's diaries, this relationship becomes even more complex. Photographs are placed alongside words, drawings, other photographs, fragments of thought. They are revisited, rearranged, reproduced and transformed. Memory becomes an active creative process rather than a passive act of preservation.

The use of Xerox is especially interesting in this respect. Reproduction here is not simply a means of copying an original. It becomes part of the artistic language itself. The texture, the imperfections, the altered colors, the materiality of the pages all contribute to the emotional experience of the work. The diaries remind us that photographs have a physical existence, and that the way we handle, sequence and preserve them can be as meaningful as the images themselves.

In an era when billions of photographs circulate through our screens, when images are increasingly detached from physical objects and, with artificial intelligence, can even be generated without any corresponding lived experience, this feels particularly significant.

We photograph everything, store everything, share everything. Yet how often do we return to those images and give them the attention necessary to become part of our memory? Mario's diaries speak instead of time spent looking, selecting, arranging, touching and remembering: the physical labor of creating meaning from the fragments of one's existence.

And perhaps this is why that small gallery in Paris was so crowded with young people.

I don't think their fascination was simply nostalgic. Nostalgia implies a desire to return to something we have lost, but many of those visitors had never known the world these diaries describe. Perhaps what they were responding to was something more immediate and universal: the evidence of a real life, with all its beauty, contradictions, intimacy and imperfections.

We often discuss the signature of a photographer in terms of light, composition, color or technique. But perhaps the most distinctive element of an artist's visual language lies somewhere deeper, in the particular way they have experienced the world. Before an image becomes iconic, before it enters the history of photography or the collective imagination, it begins with someone looking at something, or someone, and feeling compelled to remember.

Mario Sorrenti Diaries, 1991–2000 , curated by Aaron Stern, is on view at LSD, 20 Rue de la Folie Méricourt, Paris, from November 12 to December 10, 2026.

It is the expression of a life lived."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The photographs are inseparable from the people Mario loved, the places he inhabited and the cultural atmosphere that shaped him. What emerges is not only the development of a photographic language but the formation of a sensibility."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I was particularly touched by this because I lived in New York during those same years. Mario and I belong to the same generation, and although our experiences were our own, we inhabited the same city, at the same moment, within a cultural world that was undergoing an extraordinary transformation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "New York in the 1990s was a place of intense creative exchange, where fashion, photography, music, art and nightlife constantly intersected. Perhaps this helps explain why Mario's work feels so deeply personal, even when it is created within the highly sophisticated machinery of the fashion industry."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Davide's presence in the diaries is particularly poignant. Knowing his story, these images become more than fragments of a shared youth. title: China’s Luxury Problem Is Bigger Than the Economy
subtitle: From changing attitudes toward exclusivity to the rise of domestic competitors, Chinese consumers are questioning what makes luxury worth paying for — and who gets to decide.
author: Yiling Pan
hero_image_alt: China’s Luxury Problem Is Bigger Than the Economy
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Yiling Pan.
content:
China’s luxury slowdown is proving harder to reverse than many of the industry’s biggest players had hoped.

After tentative signs of recovery, LVMH’s Fashion and Leather Goods division saw organic sales decline 5% in the third quarter of 2026, reversing a brief return to growth in the previous quarter (+1%). Gucci’s comparable sales fell 6% , weighed down partly by weak mainland Chinese traffic, while Prada Group also reported subdued footfall in the market . Even Richemont, whose jewelry houses have been among the industry’s most resilient performers, reported soft demand in mainland China , despite delivering 17% group sales growth at constant exchange rates in the six months to September.

China’s property downturn, weak consumer confidence and uncertainty over future incomes help explain the sluggish demand. But experts agree the industry’s challenges run deeper than the economic landscape. Chinese consumers are reassessing what luxury is worth — and whether the brands that once defined aspiration still deserve their custom.

“The spending capacity of affluent Chinese consumers remains intact; the criteria by which value is judged have changed,” says Wenbo Li, partner and Greater China regional lead at strategy and pricing consultancy Simon-Kucher, in response to official figures that suggest China’s luxury slowdown is unfolding against a more complex consumer backdrop. According to the National Bureau of Statistics, per capita disposable income rose 4.4% in real terms during the first nine months of 2026, while total retail sales reached RMB 41.6 trillion ($6.2 trillion) in the first 10 months, up a modest 1% year-on-year. More tellingly, retail sales of services grew 4.9%, far outpacing the 0.9% increase in goods sales.

After tentative signs of recovery, LVMH’s Fashion and Leather Goods division saw organic sales decline 5% in the third quarter.

For luxury houses accustomed to commanding a premium through heritage, exclusivity and brand recognition, the implications extend beyond weaker sales. From dissatisfaction with customer service at luxury boutiques to rising expectations for meaningful experiences and renewed appreciation of domestic craftsmanship, Chinese shoppers are increasingly willing to question the value luxury brands claim to offer.

For Western luxury executives, understanding China’s slowdown cannot neglect a more uncomfortable question: What happens when consumers no longer need Western luxury brands to tell them what is desirable?

For much of China’s luxury boom, exclusivity was not a barrier to consumption. It was the point. Luxury houses cultivated scarcity, controlled access and raised prices, making ownership a marker of social distinction. For aspirational Chinese consumers, gaining entry into this exclusive world was part of the appeal. The unwritten rules were widely accepted, which is the more one spent, the greater the access and recognition one could expect. But Chinese consumers are increasingly questioning those rules, particularly the expectation that respect and attentive service must be earned through spending.

On Xiaohongshu, an increasing number of shoppers have shared complaints about dismissive treatment in luxury boutiques, especially when sales associates perceive them as unlikely to make a purchase. In November, Chinese fashion designer Lan Yu publicly criticized the attitude of Western luxury houses in a video referencing a leading luxury brand following an earlier account of an unpleasant boutique experience. The video attracted more than five million views, 31,000 likes and over 2,800 comments, with many users sharing similar experiences of feeling judged or unwelcome in luxury stores. The response suggests that frustration with the power imbalance between brands and customers extends well beyond isolated encounters.

Yann Bozec, co-founder and managing director of consultancy YB Stratis and former president of Tapestry Asia-Pacific, questions the industry’s reliance on exclusion to create demand. “Exclusivity, by definition, means excluding people. I question whether making consumers feel excluded is a healthy or sustainable way to create desire,” he says.

The tension became particularly visible in late September, when Tiffany & Co. faced a social media backlash after a customer in Chengdu complained on Xiaohongshu that a Mid-Autumn Festival mooncake gift had been sent to another high-spending client, but they hadn’t received it. The customer, who claimed to have spent more than RMB 200,000 ($30,000) at Tiffany, was dissatisfied with the brand’s response. Their post went viral, and in the days that followed, multiple related discussions around luxury customer service reached Weibo’s trending lists, prompting wider debate about preferential treatment, customer entitlement and the relationship between luxury spending and recognition. Tiffany apologized and announced improvements to its service procedures.

What has changed is that consumers are increasingly willing to publicly challenge this system built around customer hierarchies, rather than accept it as the price of entering luxury’s world.

The disconnect is also reflected in research. Simon-Kucher’s 2025 Luxury Consumer Study found that 36% of Chinese respondents were dissatisfied with personalization, 31% with communication frequency and 30% with customer engagement effectiveness.

“The biggest disconnect is not necessarily price itself, but the gap between what luxury brands offer and what Chinese consumers perceive as valuable, particularly in terms of personalization, relevance and customer engagement,” says Wenbo Li.

Luxury brands still need exclusivity to sustain desirability. But increasingly, Chinese consumers are drawing a distinction between exclusive products and exclusionary treatment. The former may justify a premium, but the latter risks driving them away.

The challenge extends beyond how luxury brands make Chinese consumers feel about themselves. It is also about what consumers actually get in return for their spending. Today, a designer handbag no longer competes only with another handbag, but also with travel, fine dining, wellness, and cultural experiences that offer alternative forms of enjoyment and fulfillment.

“Consumers aren’t necessarily spending less. Having already experienced most of the material side of life, they are no longer paying simply for the end-product, but are more discerning about the experience journey,” says Vera Wu, director and head of commercial property, Westbund Central (a Hongkong Land property).

Simon-Kucher’s research found that more than two-thirds of surveyed Chinese consumers view luxury as a lifestyle encompassing purchases, experiences and ways of living. For luxury houses and the retail destinations that accommodate them, the implications of this are increasingly tangible. A prestigious brand name may still attract affluent customers, but it does not necessarily give them a compelling reason to return.

Hongkong Land’s Westbund Central in Shanghai offers one example of how luxury retail operators are responding. The RMB 60 billion ($9 billion) mixed-use development, with a planned gross floor area of approximately 1.7 million square meters, brings together retail, dining, wellness, cultural programming and public spaces.

Westbund Central’s opening program included a mindfulness session led by Jesse Israel in collaboration with Lululemon.

Its opening initiatives have included outdoor artistic performances, an installation by British artist Morag Myerscough and a mindfulness session led by Jesse Israel in collaboration with Lululemon. Rather than positioning shopping as the sole attraction, the development seeks to give consumers reasons to spend time in the space, even without an immediate intention to buy.

“What is emerging is a demand for knowledge, and for a journey that feels both unique and refined,” says Wu. “We aren’t filling a mall in a single quarter; we are cultivating a neighborhood over a decade.”

Perhaps the biggest challenge to luxury’s recovery in China lies in a more fundamental shift: Chinese consumers are beginning to question the definition of luxury that European houses have long dominated.

For decades, Western luxury brands served as benchmarks for taste, quality and prestige. Their heritage and craftsmanship helped establish that authority, while global recognition gave their products a status that extended well beyond their physical qualities. But as Chinese consumers become more experienced and discerning, they increasingly question how much of the premium they pay reflects the product itself and how much rests on the power of the brand name.

“At some point, the brand became more important than the product. We created an industry where the label itself became the source of value, sometimes overshadowing the craftsmanship and creativity that made luxury desirable in the first place,” says Bozec.

That critique carries particular weight in China, where a renewed appreciation of the country’s own artisanal heritage is challenging the assumption that exceptional craftsmanship and refinement must come with a European label. Long before European fashion houses became global symbols of refinement, China had developed sophisticated traditions of silk-making, jewelry and decorative craftsmanship. Today, these traditions are finding renewed relevance. Chinese designers, artisans and entrepreneurs are revisiting historical techniques and cultural references, bringing them into contemporary products, with great success.

Laopu Gold is among the most commercially successful examples of this approach. Drawing on traditional Chinese goldsmithing techniques and cultural motifs, the brand — launched in 2016 — has surged in recent years as Chinese consumers favor domestic players.

The brand reported a 60.3% increase in revenue to RMB 19.81 billion ($2.97 billion) in the first six months of the year, while net profit surged 88.2% to RMB 4.27 billion ($640.5 million). Its appeal also extends to consumers of international luxury brands. According to Frost & Sullivan research, Laopu Gold’s customer base had an average overlap of 82.4% with five leading luxury brands — Louis Vuitton, Hermès, Cartier, Bulgari and Tiffany — as of March 2026.

Laopu Gold’s success also points to a broader shift in China’s fashion and luxury landscape. A new generation of homegrown brands, such as Songmont, Pane and To Summer, is building its own aesthetic identity and attracting increasingly discerning domestic consumers without relying on Western creative directors, imported heritage, or international recognition to establish credibility. Rather than seeking validation from established European fashion capitals, these brands draw on Chinese craftsmanship, local cultural references, and a deeper understanding of domestic tastes to define desirability on their own terms.

Shoppers queue outside a Laopu Gold store. The brand’s revenue rose 60.3% to RMB 19.81 billion in the first half of the year.

This is particularly relevant in China, where sophisticated manufacturing capabilities and greater access to domestic and international alternatives have broadened consumers’ understanding of quality and design. With more points of comparison, shoppers are increasingly confident in making their own judgments about what deserves a premium today, rather than relying on established brand reputations.

“What does this product mean to me? Does it reflect my own taste and sense of style, rather than simply the status of the brand?” Bozec asks, describing the questions he believes younger consumers are bringing to luxury purchases.

Simon-Kucher’s 2025 Luxury Consumer Study provides some evidence of this diversity in consumer motivations. Some 45% of Chinese respondents were classified as “Fashion Forward Icons”, who are more experimental with their purchases, compared with 15% in Europe and 11% in the US. Another 25% were identified as “Quiet Luxury Enthusiasts”, who prioritize craftsmanship and timelessness, while just 10% fell primarily into the “Status Shoppers” category.

The findings point to a market where consumers are seeking different forms of luxury value, from creative originality and personal style to exceptional craftsmanship and lasting quality.

China’s luxury market is not short of consumers who can afford expensive products. Nor do the rise of domestic competitors and the growing appeal of experiences suggest that demand for luxury goods is disappearing. What is less certain is whether the strategies that fueled the industry’s previous expansion can deliver the same returns.

Simon-Kucher’s Li expects China’s luxury market to recover gradually, but warns that “the previous growth model built on continuous price increases and an expanding customer base is unlikely to return.”

“Ultimately, restoring demand in China requires shifting from price-led premiumization to value-led differentiation,” he adds.

That distinction carries different implications across the industry. For some houses, it will require renewed emphasis on product quality, creativity and craftsmanship. For others, the priority may be improving customer relationships or creating experiences that justify a premium beyond the product itself.

Bozec offers a broader perspective on what fashion should contribute to consumers’ lives.

It is a different proposition from selling consumers a ready-made identity through brand recognition and social status. Brands should place greater emphasis on how the product or experience improves an individual’s life. “For me, fashion is one of the tools an individual has to express himself, and even more to discover himself,” Bozec says.

Economic confidence will remain important to any sustained recovery in China’s luxury market. But an improvement in sales should not be mistaken for a restoration of the industry's previous relationship with Chinese consumers.

The generation that helped build China’s luxury boom has accumulated not only wealth, but experience, knowledge, and alternatives. Luxury houses still have the opportunity to shape their aspirations, but they can no longer take that influence for granted.

title: The New Rules for Selling Beauty in China
subtitle: Coinciding with changing perceptions of ‘Made in China’, the country’s beauty landscape is shifting from a period of general expansion to one that is hyper-selective and value-driven, with clear winners and losers.
author: Kati Chitrakorn
hero_image_alt: The New Rules for Selling Beauty in China
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Kati Chitrakorn.
content:
Since Yang Zifeng and Zhou Tiancheng launched Flower Knows in 2016, the Chinese beauty brand has captured the local market with its ultra-feminine, fairytale-inspired aesthetic. Think whimsical collections of lip glosses, blushes, and eye palettes that favor softer, buildable colors and sheerer applications, drawing on the duo’s passion for cosplay — for which they have built a sizable following in China under the stage names Baozi and Hana.

This May marked a new chapter for Flower Knows, which sold a majority stake to Proya Cosmetics as part of a RMB 351 million (roughly $52.6 million) deal — a move that reflects how far C-beauty has come, for both the acquired and the acquirer.

Founded in 2003, Proya began as a single skincare brand, offering proven active ingredients at accessible prices to China’s lower-tier cities. It expanded into a multi-brand group in the late 2010s – anchored by its 2017 IPO listing and 2019 acquisition of the Chinese makeup brand Timage. In 2024, Proya surpassed RMB 10 billion ($1 billion) in annual revenue, making it China’s largest beauty company.

Proya’s decision to acquire Flower Knows highlights its strategy to buy rather than build, as it diversifies beyond its flagship skincare brand of the same name. The group first invested in Flower Knows last August and, in May, acquired an additional stake, raising its total ownership to 51%. The move is part of Proya’s ambitious plan to become one of the top 10 global cosmetics companies by 2035, with a target of RMB 50 billion ($7.5 billion) in annual revenue. Proya’s stock jumped 5.1% on the Shanghai Stock Exchange following the announcement.

Yang Zifeng and Zhou Tiancheng launched Flower Knows in 2016.

Proya’s aim represents a bigger shift for the market. China’s beauty landscape over the past decade has evolved from low-cost dupes of Western and Korean cosmetics into a value-driven, culturally distinct global powerhouse capable of commanding serious valuations. Now, having secured majority market share at home, many C-beauty brands are setting their sights on overseas expansion and are moving past social media buzz into controlled offline retail channels to build long-term profitability and trust.

“Over the past decade, we’ve built a distinct creative identity and a passionate community. At the same time, we recognize that the beauty market is becoming more competitive and consumers are more selective about where they spend,” says Flower Knows’s global CMO Fang Gongyiliu. “That makes it even more important to invest in product innovation, operational efficiency, and sustainable brand building, rather than relying on short-term trends. Our ambition isn’t simply to become a bigger brand, but to become a more enduring one.”

China is the world’s second‐largest consumer market for cosmetics. The latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics of China shows that cosmetics retail sales in September 2026 generated RMB 39 billion ($5.85 billion), up 5.4% year-on-year. Meanwhile, cosmetic retail sales in the country between January and September 2026 totaled RMB 349 billion ($20.9 billion), up 6.1% compared to the same period in 2025.

Driving the sector are multinational legacy brands, such as Chanel Beauty, La Mer and L’Oréal (the group’s business in mainland China returned to growth in late 2025 and continued its momentum into 2026 ), and rapidly surging domestic players, like Proya, Florasis and Maogeping, which collectively command more than half the domestic market, according to the China Association of Fragrance, Flavor and Cosmetic Industries .

Hua Mantian and Freeman Ren co-launched Florasis, selling cosmetics infused with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) concepts and local craftsmanship and aesthetics.

And while K-beauty has taken the world by storm , surpassing the US to become the second-largest beauty exporter globally, Chinese consumers have generally shown little interest. It’s in part due to historical geopolitical tensions that resulted in unofficial restrictions starting in 2016 on South Korean cultural and consumer goods. K-beauty’s market share in China has fallen sharply from 66% to 20%, according to 2025 Euromonitor data. In recent years, Korean beauty conglomerate Amorepacific reported that its North American business had overtaken its China revenue.

China operates as a self-contained ecosystem distinct from Western or other Asian markets. In the latter, shoppers tend to rely heavily on physical stores like Sephora or Olive Young for product discovery and hands-on testing. China’s retail ecosystem, on the other hand, is built around native, digitally integrated super-apps, such as Baidu (China’s dominant search engine), Douyin and Xiaohongshu (which play a central role in brand discovery and reviews); transaction hubs like Taobao, Tmall, JD.com and even discount site Pinduoduo; and WeChat and Alipay (which combine messaging and mobile payments, as cash and traditional credit cards are rarely used).

“The Chinese consumer is probably not seeing all these ads on Medicube or the other dozen beauty brands that are doing very well globally,” says Cherrie Rao, a former marketing executive who recently relocated to the US after living in Beijing and Shanghai for the past decade.

Thus, local visibility is crucial. That’s why most C-beauty players start online. In 2017, when Hua Mantian and Freeman Ren co-launched Florasis, selling cosmetics infused with traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) concepts and local craftsmanship and aesthetics, they bypassed traditional brick-and-mortar retail, focusing primarily on DTC distribution via local platforms like Tmall. Flower Knows has also sold primarily through digital platforms like Taobao, where it frequently hosts livestream broadcasts and ranks among top category sellers. But reaching Chinese consumers requires more than just local platform integration.

“Over the past decade, we’ve learned that storytelling alone isn’t enough to build a lasting beauty brand,” says Flower Knows’s Fang. “We often say that our products are the most important form of content. The intricate packaging, colors, textures, and the experience of opening a product give our consumers something worth discovering and sharing… But how it performs and how it fits into their everyday routine is what helps turn that interest into a purchase.”

Florasis’s key is connecting with consumers beyond recognizable aesthetics. “‘Eastern elegance’ is more than a visual style. It represents a contemporary way of living”, a spokesperson tells Vogue Business . Indeed, while consumers in China are not a monolith and span vastly different regions and thus experiences and preferences, they share a cultural foundation — including an extraordinarily rich tradition of proverbs and idioms — that continues to deeply shape people’s moral values, social behavior and daily choices.

“I think the companies who are [driving] cultural confidence are the ones who are truly living the philosophy behind Chinese culture as well,” says Jess Tang, the founder of Dumpling, an Asia-focused brand strategy and design practice, and former head of Asia insights at forecasting firm WGSN. In C-beauty, this requires a real commitment to the community, she explains. “They’re building a business that is not just about making money, but is giving back to their country, to their hometown, to the villagers.”

Chinese fragrance houses like To Summer and Documents have built entire sensory worlds around cultural traditions and objects. Since launching in Beijing in 2018, To Summer has worked directly with local farmers to extract native botanicals like Jingmai Pu’er tea, Hubei osmanthus and Xinhui tangerine peel. Its retail spaces are often set inside restored historic courtyards and heritage buildings featuring Jingdezhen porcelain and traditional craft. Founded in Shanghai in 2021, Documents reinterprets not only traditional incense but also historical Chinese scent-wearing traditions, using knotted bag charms for its 5ml perfumes (instead of standard spray bottles).

Meanwhile, the C-beauty brand Maogeping Cosmetics has become a national success story since its launch in 2000 by the namesake makeup artist. Widely celebrated as China’s first homegrown luxury beauty brand, Maogeping broke a decades-long monopoly held by Western and Japanese cosmetics giants in China’s high-end department stores and culminated its 24-year rise with a landmark HK$2.3 billion (about $300 million) IPO in Hong Kong in December 2024, turning its founder into a billionaire. Strong momentum has continued following its listing, with the company reporting 2025 full-year revenues of RMB 5.1 billion ($757 million), up 30% year-over-year.

At the heart of Maogeping’s approach is education. While most beauty brands in China prioritize e-commerce, Mao invested in hundreds of department store counters across China, using these sites not simply as points of sale but as beauty studios where trained consultants offered personalized makeup lessons and demonstrations. The company also runs its own school, teaching makeup artistry, styling, and image design, across 11 cities in China, including Beijing, Hangzhou, Chongqing and Wuhan. In Tang’s view, this contributes to the local ecosystem. “I find that powerful because, from an Asian perspective, you have to give back as much in order to grow.”

Riding the wave of cultural pride — dubbed the “guochao” movement, where Chinese millennials and Gen Z actively support domestic brands — has helped C-beauty brands to bypass the slower growth typical of new companies.

But beyond growing national confidence, there has also been a major leap in the quality, design and innovation of C-beauty products over the past decade. Western or Korean brands simply “cannot keep up”, says Linda Yu, the general manager of Red Ant Asia, which advises global brands including Creed, Moncler, Charlotte Tilbury and Byredo on navigating China’s digital landscape and overseas retailers on which C-beauty labels to stock.

Rather than copying Western formulas, domestic companies such as Giant Biogene and Bloomage Biotech (which has backed Rao’s newly launched brand, Alaris) invest heavily in proprietary R&D. Florasis, Flower Knows and Perfect Diary have turned packaging into collectible art. And brands including Judydoll (with its metal-wand “curling iron” mascara), Joocyee (for its high-performance lip formulas and jelly highlighters) and Winona (whose formulations are tailored to sensitive skin) have invented viral, functional products that Western competitors struggle to match.

Brands such as Joocyee, known for its high-performance lip formulas and jelly highlighters, have invented viral, functional products that Western competitors struggle to match.

Among C-beauty’s bright spots are color cosmetics, fragrance and beauty tools, of which online sales, tracked from January to September 2025, rose 5.4% to RMB 94.7 billion ($14.2 billion), compared to skincare, which remains the dominant category but fell 0.8% to RMB 207.8 billion ($31.2 billion), according to the latest data from Moojing, a Beijing-based consumer intelligence platform that tracks online sales across APAC.

However, amid China’s wider economic slowdown, “the overall guochao halo is fading,” warns Yu – not because Chinese consumers are returning to foreign brands, but because surface-level patriotism is no longer enough to sell a product. Thus, she says, “distinctiveness” remains key. Ellie Thorpe, director at intelligence firm Kantar BrandZ, agrees, noting that the strongest players in China compete on a point of view and give customers “a clear reason to choose them”.

Brands must also contend with changing beauty standards. While a fair, youthful and highly filtered look — coined by locals as 网红脸 wang hong lian, or “influencer face” — has long been the dominant beauty aesthetic, experts say this ideal is declining in favor of natural body types, healthy complexion and “no makeup” makeup. “I think beauty standards are becoming more diverse,” says Rao, attributing the shift to the influx of K-pop and American culture on apps like Xiaohongshu. “There are now women who want to have sun-kissed skin or draw on freckles. They want to look healthy and natural.”

Amid shifting consumer sentiment and intensifying local competition, domestic brands are also looking to offline retail channels, including overseas, for new pockets of growth. This indicates their ambition to compete on sustainable new customer acquisition and retention, rather than aggressive discounting via major local shopping events like Double 11 (also known as Singles’ Day), 520, Golden Week, and Qixi. Instead of chasing one-time bargain hunters, the focus now is on converting buyers into high-value repeat customers through prestige counters and mainstream retail partnerships.

From heritage festivals to digital shopping bonanzas, 2025 presents several opportunities to engage with China’s fast-changing market.

Florasis opened its first flagship in Hangzhou in 2022 and its first overseas store in Tokyo in 2025. Today, it is stocked by retailers in over 110 countries and regions, including Samaritaine Paris Pont Neuf in Paris, Skin Cupid in London, and Mall of the Emirates in Dubai. Meanwhile, Flower Knows expanded to Boots in the UK this March and physical Ulta stores in the US as of September. At home, it has entered specialty retailers such as Wow Colour (China’s answer to Sephora) and, in October, opened its first global flagship store on Huaihai Middle Road in Shanghai. China remains Flower Knows’s largest market overall, but the US has become its biggest internationally, Fang says.

Whether C-beauty can build lasting recognition outside of its home country remains to be seen.

But ultimately, the industry’s glow-up points to a bigger change, one where China is no longer a low-cost manufacturer and imitator, but a global powerhouse driven by original science, intricate design and innovation. See, for example, adjacent consumer industries like automobiles: China now leads the global EV industry, producing a majority of the world's electric cars and even collaborating with top European fashion figures like Kim Jones.

“The idea is that the Chinese population should be creating things that are our own instead of mimicking trends in Korea or elsewhere, whether it’s politics or culture,” says Rao. “I see a shift where China has gone from being the world’s factory to becoming the world’s lab.”

title: Who Will Win the Chinese Sportswear Race?
subtitle: China’s sportswear market is building speed. Can domestic brands overtake their Western counterparts?
author: Ashley Ogawa Clarke
hero_image_alt: Who Will Win the Chinese Sportswear Race?
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Ashley Ogawa Clarke.
content:
Birding, surfing, camping, hiking, paddleboarding, basketball, yoga, weightlifting… in 2026, the demand for physical and outdoor activities is booming in China, and the country’s sportswear market is growing to meet it.

China’s sportswear market is worth $66.7 billion, according to Euromonitor, and is expected to reach over $73 billion by 2028. Though still dwarfed by the US sportswear market, which currently sits at $168 billion, China’s market is growing faster. As local consumers become more active and health-conscious, brands are expanding in what is fast becoming a large and increasingly diversified landscape.

“The sportswear market in China is moving from volume to specialization, led by growing demand for technical outdoor products, trail-running footwear and activity-specific apparel,” says Marguerite Le Rolland, Euromonitor’s head of footwear and apparel. “At the same time, Chinese companies are making the transition from manufacturing for global brands to building global brands of their own.”

The rise in physical activity — helped along by the government’s Healthy China 2030 initiative, a major strategy launched in 2016 — is also having a knock-on effect on what people want to wear. “Overall, there’s a shift in status-signaling in China, from the new-money big logo look, to the old money hobby and lifestyle-driven status,” says Allison Malmsten, China strategy consultant at Daxue. “As a result, we see white-collar office workers now sporting Arc’teryx and Descente to the office, rather than a luxury logo.”

While China’s sportswear market is ripe with opportunity, some Western megabrands are facing headwinds amid more selective consumer sentiment and a boom in domestic players. Nike’s Greater China business has suffered, with Q1 2027 revenue falling 26% in the region, while

China was a growth engine for Lululemon post-pandemic, but revenues in the region fell 2% in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Adidas, after some difficult years in the region, is staging a recovery, with Greater China sales up 15% in the first nine months of the year. Meanwhile, more nimble local brands like Anta Sports are building multi-brand portfolios that are quickly gaining market share, with HSBC analysts calling Anta a “clear winner” over Nike for its higher profit margins in a recent research report shared with Vogue Business .

The first Anta Market fashion sports concept store in Shanghai. According to HSBC analysts, Anta is a “clear winner” over Nike for its higher profit margins in a recent research report.

The tension between legacy incumbents and newer players is playing out in an increasingly fragmented market. The age of the general fitness buyer in China is over, and a more segmented landscape has emerged. “Five years ago, the market was driven by basic, all-purpose gear,” says Eva Zhang, project director of ISPO China, a leading sportswear trade fair. “Today, niche tracks like trail running, lightweight hiking, and even pet outdoor gear are booming.” Some Western labels are benefiting from the shift: outdoor label Arc’teryx’s parent company, Amer Sports, saw 30.4% growth in Greater China for Q3 2026.

ISPO’s Brand Showcase in Beijing in January 2027 aims to bring “international buyers closer to Chinese innovation,” says Zhang.

“Consumers have become far more knowledgeable and sophisticated about product function, materials and technical details,” adds Running Xie, general manager of insight, ideas and increment at Buy Quickly, a leading omnichannel e-commerce platform. “They demand category-specific technical gear, not one-size-fits-all athletic apparel.”

As less agile, more generalized incumbents struggle to adapt, local brands are stepping in to meet demand. Kailas, which specializes in trail running gear, is forecasting $1.7 billion in revenue this year. Xie points to major local brand Mobi Garden (camping gear), and mid-sized or smaller independent designer brands like UTO (known for fashionable base layers) and Tajezzo (functional backpacks), as just a few examples of names that have cornered a niche. They satisfy demand for sport-specific, professional-grade performance wear, which — even when it’s casual — helps telegraph knowledge, participation and status.

“Even if they don’t do it in a professional way, they need to have the professional item,” says Sophia Dumenil, co-founder of The Chinese Pulse. “It’s cooler to have the total look. It’s also a way to show that you take care of yourself. The new beauty standard [for women] that’s emerging is not about being delicate; it’s about being fit and healthy.”

At the same time, consumers also want sportswear they can wear when they’re not doing sports. Feng Chen Wang, who works with Under Armour on ‘Rebel Daughter’, a line of China-inspired sporty casualwear, has observed a blurring of boundaries between sportswear and everyday clothing in China — especially among Gen Z. “Sport isn’t a slot in the day; it lives inside the day,” says the designer. “To reach a younger consumer, the garment has to be something you can wear into your life first.”

Feng Chen Wang and Under Armour’s collaboration ‘Rebel Daughter’ is a line of China-inspired sporty casualwear.

The designer has focused on creating garments that aren’t built for competition but “light movement” — sporty-looking tracksuits with a contemporary fashion edge. “Young people’s lives now are looser, more varied, and they want convenience. Nobody needs to change three or five outfits a day,” she says. “The lines between occasion, function and fashion are being folded into one.”

Beneunder, a brand that makes sun-protective clothing, highlights the potential of the shift. “Sun protection has evolved beyond a seasonal beauty concern into a broader lifestyle category,” says Cindy Gong, Beneunder’s affiliate marketing manager. “Consumers increasingly want products that combine protection with comfort, breathability, lightweight design, and style. We believe this reflects a wider shift toward functional clothing that can transition naturally between everyday life and outdoor activities.”

Beneunder, which makes sun-protective clothing, sees sun protection becoming “a broader lifestyle category” rather than a seasonal beauty concern, says affiliate marketing manager Cindy Gong.

As sportswear branches out into these various specialties, consumer motivations can be separated into what strategists at forecasting agency WGSN think of as ‘Push’ (think competitive sports like trail running, tennis and Hyrox) and ‘Pause’ (more restorative activities like birding, fishing and paddleboarding that can help overworked people to decompress). “Right now, everything falls into those two camps,” says Alison Ho, APAC strategist at WGSN. “Chinese consumers are either chasing a personal best or chasing peace. The brands that win will know which one they’re selling to.”

Local brands in China are gaining influence, but they must still compete with international names that are stepping up their strategies to capture the Chinese market. Following a successful online launch in August, Alo Yoga has laid out plans to open nine stores across Greater China, while Reebok has set a target to open up to 200 outlets in mainland China by 2029.

To successfully capture the market and connect with local consumers, cultural nuance is key. Juliette Duveau, who runs The Chinese Pulse with Dumenil, points to Adidas’s collaborations with local designers, including Shuting Qiu and Edison Chen, and Nike, which has incorporated traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) into multiple products and activations in the country, for instance, with the Jordan brand, which hosted a TCM-themed pop-up in Shanghai in partnership with BMX rider Nigel Sylvester. Nike also plans to design and develop 50% of its Nike Sportswear and Jordan products sold in China locally by fiscal 2030, per Reuters . At a time when many international brands face heat in China for cultural missteps, this kind of hyper-localized approach cuts through. “Just collaborating with a name today is not enough. The concept needs to be super-matching with what you want to do,” says Duveau.

The Adidas Originals Neo-Chinese SS27 collection.

These localized activations are just the surface and hint at a larger macro shift in supply chains, with more products designed in China rather than just manufactured there. Nike’s announcement of its 2030 manufacturing goals is meant to better integrate into the market. “It’s no longer just placing orders and OEM manufacturing, but moving towards co-creation and joint R&D,” says ISPO’s Zhang. “China is transforming from the world’s factory into a global innovation engine.”

At the same time, international giants face a rising tide of Chinese brands making their own inroads. In 2026, NBA player Stephen Curry signed a 10-year partnership worth a reported $400 million with Li-Ning, with Curry’s first shoe for the brand slated for release in 2027. Anta, China’s largest sportswear company, which opened its first US flagship in California in February, is implementing a broad strategy of investing in international sportswear businesses. It recently became the largest shareholder in Puma and is also the largest shareholder of Amer Sports (which itself owns Salomon and Wilson alongside Arc’teryx). “It brings brands that are already established and reassuring in terms of their sports authenticity and innovation capabilities directly into their ecosystem,” says Duveau. “It also helps them to build credibility and legitimacy, which maybe gives Anta leverage to make their own brand more premium in the future.”

Gorpcore label Uppervoid sorts its gear by altitude and trip length. “It’s specialists versus generalists,” says Ho.

Zhang says that while Chinese brands have the hard power to compete globally, the challenges are clear. “The stereotype of Made in China takes time to break, and moving from what is cost-effective to what is value-driven is the core challenge,” she says. In January 2027, ISPO will hold a Brand Showcase in Beijing, with exhibitors spanning outdoor and snowsports to camping and general lifestyle. “Our aim is to help Chinese brands amplify their brand value globally while bringing international buyers closer to Chinese innovation,” says Zhang.

While the big names battle for global relevance, some believe smaller brands will come to the fore. “The most exciting energy is often below Anta and Li-Ning,” says Ho. She points to Aonijie, the official hydration partner of the UTMB World Series (a trail running circuit), and a new wave of design-forward labels that take a granular approach. Uppervoid, a gorpcore label whose slogan is “In Nature We Trust”, sells mountaineering gear that is segmented by altitude, and trekking clothing filtered by how many days you plan to spend on the road.

“This is no longer China versus the West,” says Ho. “It’s specialists versus generalists.”
