Following a successful online launch in August, Alo Yoga has laid out plans to open nine stores across Greater China, while Reebok has set a target to open up to 200 outlets in mainland China by 2029."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To successfully capture the market and connect with local consumers, cultural nuance is key. Juliette Duveau, who runs The Chinese Pulse with Dumenil, points to Adidas\u2019s collaborations with local designers, including Shuting Qiu and Edison Chen, and Nike, which has incorporated traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) into multiple products and activations in the country, for instance, with the Jordan brand, which hosted a TCM-themed pop-up in Shanghai in partnership with BMX rider Nigel Sylvester. Nike also plans to design and develop 50% of its Nike Sportswear and Jordan products sold in China locally by fiscal 2030, per Reuters. At a time when many international brands face heat in China for cultural missteps, this kind of hyper-localized approach cuts through. \u201cJust collaborating with a name today is not enough. The concept needs to be super-matching with what you want to do,\u201d says Duveau."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6b005194ff7127318758a893/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/11-23-26-CHINA-SPORTSWEAR-BOOM-vogue-business-story-inline-4.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Adidas Originals Neo-Chinese SS27 collection."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These localized activations are just the surface and hint at a larger macro shift in supply chains, with more products designed in China rather than just manufactured there. Nike\u2019s announcement of its 2030 manufacturing goals is meant to better integrate into the market. \u201cIt\u2019s no longer just placing orders and OEM manufacturing, but moving towards co-creation and joint R&D,\u201d says ISPO\u2019s Zhang. \u201cChina is transforming from the world\u2019s factory into a global innovation engine.\u201d"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the same time, international giants face a rising tide of Chinese brands making their own inroads. In 2026, NBA player Stephen Curry signed a 10-year partnership worth a reported $400 million with Li-Ning, with Curry\u2019s first shoe for the brand slated for release in 2027. Anta, China\u2019s largest sportswear company, which opened its first US flagship in California in February, is implementing a broad strategy of investing in international sportswear businesses. It recently became the largest shareholder in Puma and is also the largest shareholder of Amer Sports (which itself owns Salomon and Wilson alongside Arc\u2019teryx). \u201cIt brings brands that are already established and reassuring in terms of their sports authenticity and innovation capabilities directly into their ecosystem,\u201d says Duveau. \u201cIt also helps them to build credibility and legitimacy, which maybe gives Anta leverage to make their own brand more premium in the future.\u201d"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6b005195f07ad804d3cf140c/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/11-23-26-CHINA-SPORTSWEAR-BOOM-vogue-business-story-inline-3.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gorpcore label Uppervoid sorts its gear by altitude and trip length. \u201cIt\u2019s specialists versus generalists,\u201d says Ho."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Zhang says that while Chinese brands have the hard power to compete globally, the challenges are clear. \u201cThe stereotype of Made in China takes time to break, and moving from what is cost-effective to what is value-driven is the core challenge,\u201d she says. In January 2027, ISPO will hold a Brand Showcase in Beijing, with exhibitors spanning outdoor and snowsports to camping and general lifestyle. \u201cOur aim is to help Chinese brands amplify their brand value globally while bringing international buyers closer to Chinese innovation,\u201d says Zhang."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While the big names battle for global relevance, some believe smaller brands will come to the fore. \u201cThe most exciting energy is often below Anta and Li-Ning,\u201d says Ho. She points to Aonijie, the official hydration partner of the UTMB World Series (a trail running circuit), and a new wave of design-forward labels that take a granular approach. Uppervoid, a gorpcore label whose slogan is \u201cIn Nature We Trust\u201d, sells mountaineering gear that is segmented by altitude, and trekking clothing filtered by how many days you plan to spend on the road."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "\u201cThis is no longer China versus the West,\u201d says Ho. \u201cIt\u2019s specialists versus generalists.\u201d"}]

title: Read Vogue’s Best Dressed Cover Interview with Connor Storrie
subtitle: “I love it,” Storrie says of fashion. “It’s just self-expression.”
author: Vogue
hero_image_alt: Read Vogue’s Best Dressed Cover Interview with Connor Storrie
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Vogue.
content:
It was only a year ago that his various states of dishabille—often in acrobatic coital arrangements with his Heated Rivalry costar Hudson Williams—made him an object of something close to social media psychosis. Over the next 12 months, this 26-year-old actor—originally from Odessa, Texas, and more latterly a starry-eyed Hollywood hopeful waiting tables in Los Angeles—left a different impression. At the Golden Globes he wore a sharp-shouldered suit and aviators; at the Met , a polka-dot shoulder-baring halter-neck top and high-waist pleated pants. In June, front row at Saint Laurent, the house where he serves as an ambassador , he was seated next to Madonna, in PVC boots and a knit vest; a few months earlier, at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party, his ensemble was a body-hugging transparent turtleneck and diamond-encrusted Tiffany & Co. link necklace.

On a recent visit to our offices, Storrie arrived in casual attire before sweeping into the fashion closet and shimmying into a pair of fluid trousers, a snug T-shirt, and a blouson-style jacket, giving himself an assured once-over. “I love it,” he said about such transformations. “It’s just self-expression.” Read on for an excerpt of his conversation with Vogue ’s Chloe Malle on The Run-Through —which ranged from Storrie’s punk roots and his adoration of Parker Posey to his side hustle in “provocateur” photography, and beyond. Listen to the full episode below. — Max Berlinger, senior fashion news editor

Loewe jacket, shirt, and trousers. Styled by Spencer Singer.

Prada trousers. Styled by Spencer Singer.

HEADSPACE “I’m always doing something—I’m either making music or doing photos. It’s not like acting or filmmaking where I feel like that’s my purpose,” says Storrie, here in Gucci. “This stuff is a kind of doodling.”

Chloe Malle: For Vogue ’s Best Dressed cover story, we wanted to pick someone who was part of the moment we’re in, who took risks and had fun with it. You seem to have just launched into fashion….

Connor Storrie: I’ve always loved to express myself. I think growing up, I had a plethora of chapters in terms of my clothing and hair—and just my physical appearance. But before doing red carpets and going to events and fashion shows, I never considered fashion the way I do now. It was really James Yardley, my stylist, who helped me see how much time and thought and effort went into all of it—and now I love it.

Storrie in a Raggedy Threads quarter-zip. Prada trousers and bag. Lii hood. Falke socks and Church’s shoes.

Tell me about the shoot that accompanies this interview—I heard you were dancing a lot on set. Were there any songs that got you moving?

Everyone always asks me on set, “What do you want to listen to?” And I’m like, “Honestly, just play whatever.” I like to match whatever’s going on rather than putting on my thing. My thing would be a little too aggressive—it’s like weird, hard electronic stuff. I listen to a lot of, um…actually, it’s very popular in Eastern Europe, it’s called bochka.

Oh wow. Did you get into that when you were in a Heated Rivalry headspace, or was that pre?

No, I’ve liked this for a really long time—probably eight years? I’ve always listened to independent artists on SoundCloud, and I just went down this weird rabbit hole.

Storrie wears a Versace jacket. Raggedy Threads tank top. Loro Piana turtleneck, trousers, and shoes.

What makes you feel comfortable when you’re in front of the camera? Is that an easy place for you to be?

I love photo shoots—I used to do photo shoots with my friends. I’d do these really interesting self-portraits too when I was in high school. I’ve always been kind of a photographer.

Have you done shoots recently?

I did one probably a year ago—they’re kind of editorial, but they’re also just…provocateur stuff. I’m always doing something—I’m either making music or doing photos. It’s not like acting or filmmaking where I feel like that’s my purpose. This stuff is a kind of doodling. It’s my way of just staying active.

What’s your relationship with New York like? You’re originally from Texas but you live in LA—do you have a checklist of things you always do here, or do you just explore?

I just walk around, honestly. I usually stay—is it in or on Manhattan? I always get called out.

Oof. Yeah, that’s it. I talk and people go, “Not from here, huh bud?”

Miu Miu pants and shorts. Falke socks. Church’s shoes.

Calvin Klein Collection shirt, The Row trousers, Falke socks, and New Balance sneakers.

I want to know about your first fashion memory—do you remember when you understood the power of getting dressed, or found an item you couldn’t live without?

I’ve always fixated on a single pair of shoes, and then worn that pair into the ground. I remember being in preschool and having these moon boots—Napoleon Dynamite boots—and feeling like, This is me.

What’s your outfit right now?

YSL jeans. They have, like, blood stains on them—not super visible, but I just wear those jeans every single day—and a black shirt, and these Onitsukas.

Do you remember your first major fashion purchase?

Do you know the brand New Rock? I was punk in, like, 2018—​that was my thing. I used to wear these cargo camo shorts past the knee, and I would wear three-inch platform curb-stomper boots that went halfway up the calf. I think they were $450, which was a lot at the time. I was in a crew that was into techno, maybe that’s where my thing for deep-industrial music started. They were very popular amongst this crowd I was hanging with.

Was there any sort of goth makeup happening?

Nope—I had long hair that I never brushed, and I would just wear, like, cool cutoff shirts.

Is there anything you’ve worn recently that you’ve regretted?

No—I rock things with confidence. I mean, that’s the thing about fashion, right? You cannot take in what anyone else has to say. I don’t go online; I don’t pay attention to it—don’t have the apps on my phone and I don’t listen to it. When I cut my hair, I didn’t know anyone was having a negative reaction until these fans came up to me and were like, “You know what people are calling you online, right?” And I was like, “No, I actually have no idea.” And they were like, “Buzznor. You’re Buzznor.” And I was like, “That’s kind of silly.” I just didn’t care about it. People don’t know what they’re talking about, you know?

That’s very mature of you.

But I also try not to hold anything too precious.

Do you and Hudson Williams talk about what you’re wearing before you’re on a red carpet together? Do your styles diverge?

We don’t talk, but I think there’s been a natural cohesion. We are very cut from the same cloth, so there’s a lot of synchronicity. I think Hudson always looks good, but he’s also different than me—there’s something street style or edgy about what he does, and I always kind of envy that.

How often are you guys in touch?

Right now we’re filming [the next season of Heated Rivalry ], so I literally live with him, which is amazing. We were at this hotel, which was a brilliant hotel, but I just…. I needed a washing machine. I needed a kitchen.

LEANING IN “I rock things with confidence. I mean, that’s the thing about fashion, right?” says Storrie, here in Ferragamo. “You cannot take in what anyone else has to say.”

You’ve always wanted to be an actor. When you were 12, you had a YouTube channel, Actorboy222.

That was just a handful of videos where I was alone in my room at my dad’s house in Odessa, Texas. It was when people would go on YouTube and create videos talking to the camera and doing skits or characters or whatever. And so I was like, “I’ll do that.” One of those videos is what drunk people do when they get home. It’s 12-year-old me pretending to be drunk. In the video, I just get the remote control, and for 30 seconds, I sit in silence and watch TV.

Which honestly is what drunk people do.

But then I got locked out of that account, and so I couldn’t take those off. And now they live on the internet.

Ferragamo jacket. Celine shoes.

When we met at a Tiffany dinner earlier this year, I was so excited to hear about your experience in the clown community in Los Angeles. What is it about that experience that has stayed with you?

I think clown and performance art—I say performance art, not just clown, because there’s a lot of stuff that we did that wasn’t traditional clown—taught me that there’s a line where something can be simultaneously funny and sad; something can be both sexy and bizarre. I love operating in the gray parts of art and entertainment, where you don’t really know what this is, but it’s just kind of off so that it’s interesting. People will do performances where they get up and just look at the audience for three minutes and not say anything, and it can be scary and off-putting, and then two seconds later you’re laughing because you can’t help but break the ice. And then it goes on for another minute and you’re like, “Oh, this is kind of beautiful and vulnerable.” I love that gray space.

Loewe shirt and trousers. Prada shoes.

Burberry coat, Prada sweater, Society Archive vintage trousers, Nike headband, and Danned boots.

You went to the Met Gala for the first time this year, and you went to the Golden Globes, the Vanity Fair Oscar Party—have you had any surreal encounters or met any of your heroes?

I was kind of in love with Parker Posey, and I met her. She was in a movie that was really inspirational to me— The Doom Generation, this Gregg Araki movie—and ever since I saw it I was like, Who is this person? I went down the whole Christopher Guest rabbit hole of seeing her in Waiting for Guffman and Best in Show, and so meeting her was like, Wow. The people that I get starstruck by are never the bigger-than-life stars, like the Nicole Kidmans or the Meryl Streeps—the people that everyone knows. I get starstruck by people who were important to me. Like, when I met Lake Bell—I remember her in this weird rom-com, Over Her Dead Body, that I watched all the time with my sister growing up. I met her and was like, “Oh my God, it’s you—you’re real. You’re real.” You know what I mean?

You just filmed Halina Reijn’s upcoming film, Please, with Gracie Abrams. I also love everyone else in that—Lola Tung, David Jonsson, Tom Burke…. What was the vibe off the set or after-hours?

I love, love, love Gracie Abrams. She gave me the most beautiful gift I think I’ve ever been given: this Tiffany necklace with these antique charms, these little symbols of the characters that we play. It was just so cool.

WHAT A SPORT Calvin Klein Collection tank top and cummerbund. Dries Van Noten shorts.

Do you think you’re going to keep learning Russian when Heated Rivalry is over?

No, it’s crazy. With the amount of time that I’ve spent on it, you’d think I would be able to speak by now—but Russian is hard. It’s so sexy, that language. But so incredibly hard.

You’ve dabbled in other languages too, yes?

My French used to be really good, and now it’s okay. I can speak some Spanish from growing up in Texas and living in California, and I think that’s what I’m gonna tackle next. In my next little period of time that I have to myself, I’m gonna take Spanish lessons.

I wish you well with your Spanish.

Thank you. Gracias. Muchas gracias.

Comme des Garçons T-shirt.

Storrie in a Dior suit and shirt. Dunhill bow tie. Celine shoes.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

In this story: makeup, Yumi Lee; grooming, Kumi Craig; tailor, Tae Yoshida.

Produced by Hen’s Tooth Productions. Set design: Javier Irigoyen.

I remember being in preschool and having these moon boots\u2014Napoleon Dynamite boots\u2014and feeling like, This is me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What\u2019s your outfit right now?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "YSL jeans. They have, like, blood stains on them\u2014not super visible, but I just wear those jeans every single day\u2014and a black shirt, and these Onitsukas."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Do you remember your first major fashion purchase?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Do you know the brand New Rock? I was punk in, like, 2018\u2014\u200bthat was my thing. I used to wear these cargo camo shorts past the knee, and I would wear three-inch platform curb-stomper boots that went halfway up the calf. I think they were $450, which was a lot at the time. I was in a crew that was into techno, maybe that\u2019s where my thing for deep-industrial music started. They were very popular amongst this crowd I was hanging with."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2cd7ae5f2b4d1693866d/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_PENTAX_0088_01_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Was there any sort of goth makeup happening?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Nope\u2014I had long hair that I never brushed, and I would just wear, like, cool cutoff shirts."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Is there anything you\u2019ve worn recently that you\u2019ve regretted?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "No\u2014I rock things with confidence. I mean, that\u2019s the thing about fashion, right? You cannot take in what anyone else has to say. I don\u2019t go online; I don\u2019t pay attention to it\u2014don\u2019t have the apps on my phone and I don\u2019t listen to it. When I cut my hair, I didn\u2019t know anyone was having a negative reaction until these fans came up to me and were like, \u201cYou know what people are calling you online, right?\u201d And I was like, \u201cNo, I actually have no idea.\u201d And they were like, \u201cBuzznor. You\u2019re Buzznor.\u201d And I was like, \u201cThat\u2019s kind of silly.\u201d I just didn\u2019t care about it. People don\u2019t know what they\u2019re talking about, you know?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That\u2019s very mature of you."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But I also try not to hold anything too precious."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2cd407fbf79c58877a61/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_PENTAX_0100_02_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Do you and Hudson Williams talk about what you\u2019re wearing before you\u2019re on a red carpet together? Do your styles diverge?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We don\u2019t talk, but I think there\u2019s been a natural cohesion. We are very cut from the same cloth, so there\u2019s a lot of synchronicity. I think Hudson always looks good, but he\u2019s also different than me\u2014there\u2019s something street style or edgy about what he does, and I always kind of envy that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How often are you guys in touch?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Right now we\u2019re filming [the next season of Heated Rivalry], so I literally live with him, which is amazing. We were at this hotel, which was a brilliant hotel, but I just\u2026. I needed a washing machine. I needed a kitchen."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2cd6bc8d470c81dc99fe/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_Shot_05_103_03_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "LEANING IN \u201cI rock things with confidence. I mean, that\u2019s the thing about fashion, right?\u201d says Storrie, here in Ferragamo. \u201cYou cannot take in what anyone else has to say.\u201d"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You\u2019ve always wanted to be an actor. When you were 12, you had a YouTube channel, Actorboy222."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That was just a handful of videos where I was alone in my room at my dad\u2019s house in Odessa, Texas. It was when people would go on YouTube and create videos talking to the camera and doing skits or characters or whatever. And so I was like, \u201cI\u2019ll do that.\u201d One of those videos is what drunk people do when they get home. It\u2019s 12-year-old me pretending to be drunk. In the video, I just get the remote control, and for 30 seconds, I sit in silence and watch TV."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Which honestly is what drunk people do."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But then I got locked out of that account, and so I couldn\u2019t take those off. And now they live on the internet."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2cd59475a8cf065d40a4/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_Shot_03_201_02_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2cd779ab543e4ed679cb/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_Shot_05_237_01_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ferragamo jacket. Celine shoes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When we met at a Tiffany dinner earlier this year, I was so excited to hear about your experience in the clown community in Los Angeles. What is it about that experience that has stayed with you?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I think clown and performance art\u2014I say performance art, not just clown, because there\u2019s a lot of stuff that we did that wasn\u2019t traditional clown\u2014taught me that there\u2019s a line where something can be simultaneously funny and sad; something can be both sexy and bizarre. I love operating in the gray parts of art and entertainment, where you don\u2019t really know what this is, but it\u2019s just kind of off so that it\u2019s interesting. People will do performances where they get up and just look at the audience for three minutes and not say anything, and it can be scary and off-putting, and then two seconds later you\u2019re laughing because you can\u2019t help but break the ice. And then it goes on for another minute and you\u2019re like, \u201cOh, this is kind of beautiful and vulnerable.\u201d I love that gray space."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://assets.vogue.com/photos/6afb2d250f4428a779f972d1/master/w_1600%2Cc_limit/261011_SCHORR_VOGUE_PENTAX_0029-1_02_RGB.jpg", "caption": "Photography curated via Vogue Archives."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Loewe shirt and trousers. The people that I get starstruck by are never the bigger-than-life stars, like the Nicole Kidmans or the Meryl Streeps\u2014the people that everyone knows. I get starstruck by people who were important to me. Like, when I met Lake Bell\u2014I remember her in this weird rom-com, Over Her Dead Body, that I watched all the time with my sister growing up. title: Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe’s Tender Record of a Vanishing Amazon
subtitle: On view through March 28, 2027, “Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe” at ICA Miami brings together more than 100 works, from his earliest experiments on handmade paper in the 1990s to breathtaking installations and a newly commissioned film shaped by his recent initiation as a shaman.
author: Salomé Gómez-Upegui
hero_image_alt: Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe’s Tender Record of a Vanishing Amazon
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Salomé Gómez-Upegui.
content:
To reach his home in Mahekoto, a Yanomami community deep in the Amazon, Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe, one of the most lauded Venezuelan artists working today, first flies from Caracas to the southern town of Puerto Ayacucho. From there, it’s an eight-day journey by boat along the Orinoco River.

The village, home to around 300 people, has no electricity and no phone signal. Hakihiiwe spends his days in close communion with nature, fishing, hunting, and gathering. In a notebook, he draws everything he sees.

For the past 30 years, Hakihiiwe has been devoted to making art about his homeland. “I want to show both the grandeur of the rainforest and the quiet importance of something as delicate as an insect’s eyelash,” he says. “Every element, no matter how small, contributes to that balance and the way life functions.”

We are speaking on the occasion of his first solo museum exhibition in the US, at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami (ICA Miami), in partnership with the Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain. On view through March 28, 2027, “Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe” brings together more than 100 works spanning his decades-long career, from his earliest experiments on handmade paper in the 1990s to breathtaking installations and a newly commissioned film shaped by his recent initiation as a shaman.

For the show, Taller de Arquitectura, the Mexico City–based studio led by Mauricio Rocha Iturbide, has transformed the museum’s second floor into a space modeled after the shapono , the traditional Yanomami communal house. The works are set across modular walls in dark, earthy tones, lit by soft, filtered light, and the gallery windows have been reframed around the tree canopies outside, so “nature isn’t just an image on the wall, but an active presence within the space,” Rocha Iturbide explains.

Hakihiiwe began making art in 1992, when the Mexican artist Laura Anderson Barbata held a workshop teaching his community to craft paper by hand. That initiative eventually led to Shapono (1996), a book the Yanomami created entirely from recycled paper and thread spun from pineapple leaves. (Today, it is the earliest work in the ICA show.) Yet his relationship to art goes back to his childhood, when he watched his mother, an artisan, weave and paint baskets. “She taught me how to paint,” he says, “and words she once shared with me remain deeply important: ‘This is the path for you; you must not abandon it. In time, you will see how well things turn out.’”

Heeding his mother’s words, Hakihiiwe made art his life’s work, slowly shaping a visual language for Yanomami life and culture. To this day, he often creates paintings and prints on paper made from plant fibers or trees from his homeland. He first exhibited in Caracas in 2010, after which his work traveled the world, even reaching both the Venice Biennale and the Biennale of Sydney in 2022.

At the ICA exhibition, the artist’s near-taxonomic approach, rooted in close observation and repetition, is on striking display. One wall is covered with Kamie ya uriji pi jami Parawa ujame theperekui uriji terimi thepe komi kua (Donde yo vivo también viven todos estos animales en el Orinoco) (2018), a series of about 60 works on paper, each filled with repeated drawings in red and black ink. At first glance, they appear to be simple lines and symbols, a kind of script. Peer closer, though, and each gesture evokes an animal found in the Orinoco basin: rows of crab eyes, heron feet, ticks. Tarara (Casa de hormigas grandes) (2023) plays with perception in a similar way: red acrylic lines branch across cotton paper like a cosmic web or a map of neural pathways. What they actually trace, as the title suggests, is a house of large ants.

The pared-back quality of Hakihiiwe’s works conceals an undercurrent of urgency. The Amazon shelters much of Earth’s plant and animal life, absorbs vast amounts of carbon, and shapes weather far beyond its borders. But illegal mining, deforestation, pollution, and climate change have left it at serious risk. (Scientists estimate that about 20% of the rainforest has disappeared over the past 50 years.) “Hakihiiwe calls our attention to the ecological crisis affecting the Amazon forest, reminding us that we are all together in this problem, on a planetary scale,” says Michela Alessandrini, curator at the Fondation Cartier. “His take on this matter is brave, conscious, yet tender. His work is an important reminder of the fragility of our planet, and a representation of the manifestations it grants humans on a daily basis, if they just pay attention.”

Sheroanawe Hakihiiwe, He hupe (Mountains) , 2026. Pigmented and pressed pulp on cotton pulp and screen printing, 76 3/8 x 152 3/4 in. (194 x 388 cm), diptych. Courtesy the artist and Galería ABRA, Caracas

Elsewhere in the show, a series of landscapes offers a wider view of the ecosystems that inspire Hakihiiwe’s art. A highlight is the sprawling diptych He hupe (Mountains) (2026), made of pigmented pressed cotton pulp with screen printing that conjures the mountains of the Orinoco region. “Hakihiiwe always carries his native surroundings with him through his dreams and his art, wherever he goes… These mountains are constructed through layers of different techniques and colors, reading as an accumulation of dreamlike visions, memories, and natural elements separated across time and space,” Alessandrini adds.

Since Hakihiiwe assumed the role of shaman in 2024, dreams and visions have taken on a deeper meaning in his work. An important section of the show explores how the initiation has shaped his art. A new film, Hekura peni ware puhi aupouhe (The Spirits Wash My Face) (2026), sets kaleidoscopic drawings in motion to the sound of his own chanting, centering his bond with the spirits that visit him as he sleeps. An installation of three red shamanic poles, made on site, also speaks to the increasingly sacred dimension of his practice.

From the exhibition’s smallest ink drawings to the largest installations, the same elements return again and again. For the Yanomami, explains Gean Moreno, co-curator of the exhibition, all forms speak to one another: the cosmos to the patterns of ceremonial body paint, a feather crown to the shape of the communal house. “The pattern in the shamanic poles at the center of the exhibition space appears identical to the alligator skin of the mythical figure Irawire, who brought fire to the Yanomami,” Moreno says. “Rather than a logic of originality and representation, we have something like a circular movement of forms reiterating one another and reinforcing the overall cosmological whole at every turn.”

For Hakihiiwe, the notion of a world in which everything is part of a whole has only grown more profound since his initiation. “Now I feel a coolness in my chest, like a gentle breeze passing through,” he says. “I feel more deeply connected to the spirits, to the wind, and to the living world, and that gives me an even greater desire to create.”

title: The 16 Best Airbnbs in Palm Springs for Mid-Century Modern Devotees
subtitle: Need a desert getaway? Bookmark the 16 best Airbnbs in Palm Springs for a design-forward vacation complete with pools, palm trees, and plenty of sun.
author: Nicole Kliest
hero_image_alt: The 16 Best Airbnbs in Palm Springs for Mid-Century Modern Devotees
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Nicole Kliest.
content:
It’s an instantly recognized vignette: the San Jacinto Mountains rising in the distance, palm trees in the foreground, and a sea of mid-century modern homes dotted along the valley floor. Palm Springs is unmistakable , and its charms undeniable. It’s no wonder the glamorous desert destination has been a favored escape for Hollywood royalty for nearly a century. Beyond its numerous famous admirers (a roster that includes the likes of Elvis Presley, Lucille Ball, and Frank Sinatra) Palm Springs is also home to world-famous events, including the Coachella Music & Arts Festival , Modernism Week, and the city’s namesake International Film Festival. Where to stay for all of the above? The best Airbnbs in Palm Springs, naturally.

There are plenty of design-driven hotels throughout Palm Springs—there’s no denying that—but if you’re traveling with friends and want a home base where you can all be together (preferably beside a private pool), consider the Airbnbs below. Celebrating a special occasion, like a birthday or a bachelorette party ? These resort-style vacation rentals also fit the bill. After all, they’re no ordinary rentals: Each of these homes tells a story that speaks to Palm Springs heritage, whether it’s a William Krisel estate from circa 1959, or an elegant property that once belonged to Katharine Hepburn.

Ahead, the 16 best Airbnbs in Palm Springs for a design-forward stay in the sun.

Positioned 20 minutes from downtown Palm Springs, this 1955-era home was designed by architect Walter S. White and is a National Historic Landmark. The iconic building is easily identified by its sweeping roofline, with curvature made to mimic the San Jacinto Mountains. There’s a cedar soaking tub for relaxing evenings, and a vintage record collection to set the soundtrack for long dinners. And if you’re a nature lover, take note of the native desert garden that encircles the property.

Rooms: 1 bedroom, 2 bathrooms

Amenities: Washer/dryer, AC, indoor fireplace, dishwasher, backyard, fire pit, BBQ, pool, hot tub.

Travel back to 1963 in this luxury home; it’s one of just a handful of original properties left on the block. The interiors lean into the nostalgia with standout vignettes like a marble fireplace and a vintage windowed door. Outside, a lush yard and resort-style pool invites guests to soak in the sun, while a bar area with access to the kitchen window cements the home’s indoor-outdoor living sensibilities.

Rooms: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms

Amenities: Outdoor shower, washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, dishwasher, fire pit, BBQ, pool, hot tub, sauna.

Location: Indian Canyons Golf Resort

Brick fireplace! Saltwater pool! Douglas fir plywood cabinets! This classic 1955 ranch house has it all. The historic property is teed up well for travelers of all kinds, offering considered amenities ranging from a built-in dining booth to a work desk positioned next to a window, offering peaceful views of citrus trees.

Amenities : Bathtub, outdoor shower, washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, pool, backyard, BBQ, hot tub.

Location : Historic Tennis Club

This stylish, spacious home is located on the Indian Canyons golf course, tucked at the base of the San Jacinto mountains. There’s a pool, hot tub, fire pit, BBQ, bocce ball court, and even a stargazing deck for clear nights in the desert. On days when it’s particularly toasty, cool off with the outdoor shower—or, of course, the aforementioned swimming pool.

Rooms : 2 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms

Amenities : Washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, fire pit, outdoor furniture, BBQ, sun loungers, pool, hot tub, EV charger.

Whether you’re going for a dip in the pool or enjoying a rousing game of ping-pong, a stay at this three-bedroom home feels like a vacation. For an afternoon lounge, curl up in the sunroom (there are large sliding doors that open to the backyard), and when you’re feeling thirsty, mosey over to the wood-paneled bar area to whip up a cold drink.

Amenities : Bathtub, ping pong table, central AC and heating, indoor fireplace, outdoor furniture, fire pit, backyard, EV charger (level 2, Tesla only).

Location : Tahquitz River Estates

With its picturesque pool, outdoor dining space, and tiled fire pit, it’s little wonder this Palm Springs rental is such a favorite. You can’t beat the location, which is actually within walking distance of all the shops and restaurants the center has to offer. Inside, mid-century modern decor mingles with paintings and prints that all come together in a way that feels masterfully authentic.

Rooms : 3 bedrooms, 2 bathrooms

Amenities : Bathtub, washer/dryer, central heating, backyard, fire pit, outdoor dining area, sun lounger, private pool and hot tub

Location : Downtown Palm Springs

This mid-century home in Sunrise Park was built in 1957 by the Meiselman brothers (a duo responsible for hundreds of iconic properties in Palm Springs). Design details throughout the rental reflect its origins, including a floating stone corner fireplace and retro tiling—you’ll find plenty of color palette inspiration. (The chocolate brown-and-butter yellow kitchen is a real standout.)

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard with furniture, BBQ, pool.

Echoing the spirit of a southwestern casita, this stylish compound feels like its very own oasis in the desert. While the home is close to local restaurants and shops, there’s plenty to do on-property. Spend your time beside the pool or swinging from the hammock, and be sure to take your morning coffee to the peaceful front porch for a bit of quiet alone time before the activities of the day.

Amenities : Bathtub, outdoor shower, washer/dryer, ping pong table, central AC, indoor fireplace, heating, backyard, fire pit, outdoor furniture, hammock, BBQ, sun loungers, pool, hot tub, EV charger.

How do we love this Charles DuBois-designed home? Let us count the ways. The backyard misting system that’s a refreshing antidote to the desert heat, for starters. Then there’s the saltwater pool, all of the American mid-century and Danish modern furniture, and certainly the magnificent mountain and palm tree views. With its plum position in the Vistas Las Palmas neighborhood and history-rich design, it’s an instant favorite.

Rooms: 5 bedrooms, 5 bathrooms

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, pool, hot tub, outdoor furniture and fire pit, EV charger, backyard misting system.

Location: Vistas Las Palmas

A true historic gem, this landmark property by architect Donald Wexler is one of only seven of these homes that still exist. Katharine Hepburn purchased it from Spencer Tracy in the 1960s, and the house was a stone’s throw from the city’s famed racquet club. Spend your afternoons lounging by the kidney-shaped swimming pool and relish the opportunity of staying in this mid-century modern masterpiece.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, central AC, backyard with furniture, BBQ, fire pit, pool, EV charger.

This 1947-era home is just steps from downtown Palm Springs and sits on a large stretch of land with views of the San Jacinto Mountains. Groups looking to soak in the desert surroundings take note: there’s a ten-person jacuzzi, curtained cabana, and a saltwater pool.

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, central AC, backyard, pool and hot tub, outdoor furniture, BBQ.

This quintessential Palm Springs property was originally designed by modernist architect William Krisel in 1958; pieces inspired by the mid-century modern era dot the sunny living space. Glass walls open out to a backyard featuring a large pool, cedar hot tub, and desert succulents.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard, pool, hot tub, outdoor furniture, BBQ.

Awash in light and natural textures, this peaceful casita is a true home away from home. When you’re not enjoying the property’s easy access to the city’s restaurants and shops, unwind with a good book on the sofa, listen to records while preparing a meal in the full kitchen, or simply unwind in the tiled bathtub. The ink-blue tiled patio is another highlight for outdoor living.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, AC, indoor fireplace, backyard with furniture, BBQ.

Soak in the sun at this spacious rental in Little Beverly Hills. The home’s sliding doors lead out to a well-equipped backyard, complete with a pool, hot tub, fire pit, and BBQ. When the temperatures are scorching, the scalloped umbrella and shaded daybed will offer a poolside respite for afternoon naps.

Rooms: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathrooms

Amenities: Washer/dryer, record player, ping pong table, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard with furniture, pool, hot tub, BBQ.

Location: Little Beverly Hills

Travel back to 1959 in this striking William Krisel-designed home in the peaceful Racquet Club Estates neighborhood. The four-bedroom home comes with everything you need for a quintessential Palm Springs getaway: a heated saltwater pool with loungers, hot tub, gas BBQ, fire pit, and heaps of dining areas and hangout nooks to keep the weekend feeling festive.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, central AC, indoor fireplace, backyard with furniture, BBQ, pool, hot tub.

Location: Racquet Club Estates

Another William Krisel-designed home, this property sits on a quiet street in the historic Racquet Club Estates neighborhood less than a mile from Palm Canyon Drive. The property preserves architectural details like tongue-and-groove ceilings and exposed beams, while the exterior is surrounded by swaying palm trees and includes a pebble finish pool. (The titular “citron” comes through there too, via sunny yellow umbrellas.) Inside, floor-to-ceiling glass walls let the sun sweep across the various open-concept living spaces.

Amenities: Bathtub, washer/dryer, record player, central AC, heating, fire pit, hammock, sun loungers, pool.

title: ‘The Body’ Costumes Make for the Ultimate 2000s Period Piece
subtitle: “I sort of know all these girls, in a way,” says “The Body” costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier. “I think we all do, maybe.”
author: Hannah Jackson
hero_image_alt: ‘The Body’ Costumes Make for the Ultimate 2000s Period Piece
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Hannah Jackson.
content:
Costume designer Mirren Gordon-Crozier, who counts the mid-century Lessons in Chemistry and the hyper-contemporary Margo’s Got Money Troubles among her credits, has no trouble flitting between eras. But Netflix’s latest hit, The Body , a coming-of-age psychological drama set at a Catholic high school in 2004, posed a new challenge. “I hadn’t done that period before, even though I lived in it,” Gordon-Crozier tells Vogue. “I was about these girls’s age during that time. I sort of know all these girls, in a way. I think we all do, maybe.”

Gordon-Crozier grew up in London and moved to New York to attend Parsons School of Design, where she adapted to American culture by discerning what signaled status to her classmates. “Having a Balenciaga bag was really important, and that was my main takeaway from college,” she jokes. The City bag does indeed make an appearance, as do a host of other It bags—the Dior Saddle and Louis Vuitton x Takashi Murakami Pochette among them.

“Everything about that era was very important to me because it was also when I was 18 and understanding how you could bond with someone over fashion,” Gordon-Crozier says. Indeed, on-screen interloper Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) uses fashion to mark her shift from Pentecostal outsider to dance team member. But Gordon-Crozier notes that, although Lisbeth’s sartorial transformation follows her character arc, she ends the season still an outcast. “I think she doesn’t really know about pop culture or any sort of contemporary references at all. I think she was just emulating whatever Anya (Kristina Bogic) was doing,” she says.

A stint at Catholic school also informed Gordon-Crozier’s approach to the costumes. “The way to show your personal style is very minute, since everyone’s skirt has to be the same,” she says. Both on The Body and at her school, girls would roll or alter their skirts to raise the hemline and accessorize their uniforms with designer bags and jewelry. But Gordon-Crozier and creator Quinn Shephard gave themselves an extra challenge. “We set constraints for ourselves: no makeup, no jewelry. Only religious jewelry,” she explains.

One area where there was no room for even subtle individuality? The cutout leotards festooned with teal sequins that the Lions wear as their dance competition costumes. “The girls were not happy about those costumes, let’s just say that,” Gordon-Crozier laughs. “I’m like, You’re not supposed to be happy with them, okay? ”

The inspiration came from a surprisingly fashionable source. “I saw this image of Chloë Sevigny in a cutout black bodysuit, probably around the same year,” she says. “It was just with a low-waisted strappy thing—very early 2000s.” Et voilà: with matching dance shoes, thick nude tights in just the wrong shade (Gordon-Crozier notes they are the same brand that Hooters uses for its uniforms), and hair rhinestones, they had the perfect ugly dance costume. “We wanted it to be as tacky as possible, like dance competitions are,” she says.

Offstage, though, Gordon-Crozier assigned each of the girls on the dance team a specific celebrity or pop star to emulate. “Anya always felt like Misha Barton and Sienna Miller, Elise ( Sara Boustany ) had a lot of Devon Aoki, and then Maddie (Shirley Chen) is Hillary Duff,” she says. “We tried to define every one of them. It just makes it easier when you’re shopping and putting looks together. Everyone has their own color palette, so they’re not really clashing.”

Gordon-Crozier had a particular fondness for Elise’s edgier wardrobe. “Sara personally also has very similar tastes in a way: She likes dark and edgy designers like Comme des Garçons and Plein Sud and Diesel,” she says. It was Boustany’s personal tastes that helped bolster the character of Elise to feel less like a Y2K totem and more like a real person. “I had references for her, but I feel like what we made was more unique. It came alive in the fittings rather than completely copying references.”

title: The Best Documentaries of 2026, According to Vogue
subtitle: This year’s best documentaries spanned a wide range of subjects and themes, but every film on this list passes the same test: It asks hard questions and makes it impossible to look away.
author: Louisa Oreskes
hero_image_alt: The Best Documentaries of 2026, According to Vogue
hero_image_caption: Editorial photography via Vogue Archives. Documented by Louisa Oreskes.
content:
This year’s best documentaries spanned a wide range of subjects and themes, but every film on this list passes the same test: It asks hard questions and makes it impossible to look away.

That matters right now. The news comes at us in a relentless stream of stories about dehumanizing technology, unnecessary wars, and devastating climate collapse. It should rattle all of us. Instead, most days, we simply scroll past. These films force us to slow down, look closely, and listen to voices we may otherwise miss, like that of a young boy in West Texas who writes a play about Stalin, or Harlem Renaissance icons arguing over drinks in footage that sat untouched for 50 years.

The list is in no particular order.

Naza is one of this year’s most disturbing documentaries. In 80 minutes, set on Tel Aviv rooftops at night, with a city full of life gleaming in the background, we hear 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel—their faces and names protected by anonymity—describe the cold calculations made by themselves and others in Gaza following the October 7 attack. One soldier describes the AI tools he helped build, enabling the IDF to decide how targets are flagged, how much error is tolerated, and how many civilians—mostly women and children—it is acceptable to kill. The work is compared, more than once, to a video game.

What makes the film essential viewing is its unflinching evidence of how institutional logic sanitizes mass casualties. Despite many insisting that the film is riddled with inaccuracies, it undoubtedly raises questions that demand full answers.

In You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder follows convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, en famille, in the weeks before she goes to prison, and he strays from every rule of documentary filmmaking. He seems to have iterated the form into a new dimension— The Real Housewives of the penitentiary crossed with 60 Minutes —that is perhaps the perfect mirror to hold up to Holmes. He is also in the frame, and he’s steering hard.

Billy Evans, Holmes’s partner and the film’s undeniable villain, says something so perfectly deranged in every scene that it plays as almost scripted. Holmes professes innocence throughout, even as her behavior argues otherwise; she controls every conversation, including the ones about her control. The film never lays out the case against her but really doesn’t need to. After almost three hours in her company, you feel as worked over as any of her scammed investors.

In 1972, William Greaves threw a party at Duke Ellington’s Harlem townhouse and invited every surviving contributor to the Harlem Renaissance he could find. Aaron Douglas. Arna Bontemps. Eubie Blake. James Van Der Zee. The list goes on. Many hadn’t seen each other in decades. Fifty years later, Greaves’s son David made this film with that footage.

You can study the Harlem Renaissance in a classroom. You can read the material and revere the names. But nothing prepares you for the people, older then but still very much alive, in a living room arguing, interrupting, laughing at each other, still fighting over what it all meant. Nobody is a monument—that’s the film’s trick. It takes figures history had already embalmed and lets them be loud.

John Wilson took a workshop on how to sell a Hallmark movie, then tried to use the formula to sell a documentary about concrete. That’s technically the premise of The History of Concrete , his first feature, and it’s as close as you can get to a walk through someone else’s brain.

For the first stretch, you don’t know where you’re going. Neither, it seems, does Wilson. Then the detours start to connect. Wilson pursues the people most others would avoid: strangers mid-ramble, mid-obsession, too odd to be invented. His unpretentious point of view is singular, and what he finds is universal. Also, it’s one of the funniest films you’ll watch this year—until, without warning, it breaks your heart.

When a Witness Recants is a detailed and harrowing account of how, in 1983, three Baltimore teenagers were convicted of murdering a 14-year-old classmate for his jacket and ended up serving 36 years for a crime they never committed. In fact, Alfred Chestnut, Ransom Watkins, and Andrew Stewart made history by spending a combined 108 years in prison—the longest for a wrongful conviction in the United States. The evidence that led to their eventual exoneration sat in a police file for all that time.

The film chronicles malfeasance at every level, including a detective coercing child witnesses, an obvious other suspect who was never pursued, and staggering misconduct by judges and prosecutors. It is impossible, as a viewer, not to be moved by the weight of the final act, when the men meet with the witness—then himself a teenager—whose false testimony hijacked their lives. Ron Bishop attempts to explain his side of the story (coercion and all), and the men politely listen. But what they really want is an apology. The exchange is stilted, unsatisfactory—and perhaps that is inevitable. What was done to these men was not the work of a single scared teenager, but of a system that failed them catastrophically. To capture the emotional magnitude of such injustice is a very tall task. The documentary succeeds by trying.

Nuisance Bear follows polar bears living at the edge of a town in northern Canada, where tundra and parking lots collide. The question it asks is simple: Who is the nuisance here? Inuit elder Mike Tunalaaq Gibbons narrates, explaining how his people and the bears have been similarly disrupted—relocated and then barely tolerated within their new surroundings.

The film works most powerfully through sound. Helicopters thrum, ATVs whine, and under it all, the bears growl back. This is not a wildlife film in the usual sense. The bears are not observed in their habitat. They are watched at the fence line, where progress grinds against them.

Most nature documentaries take natural life and arrange it around a familiar narrative, finished with a neat ending. Nuisance Bear is shot like one but refuses to behave like one.

Before she was the woman who beat Donald Trump in court twice, E. Jean Carroll was Miss Cheerleader USA; a pioneering editor at Esquire , Playboy , and Outside ; and, for 26 years, the advice columnist who helped Elle readers navigate life’s mess. Ivy Meeropol’s film covers all of it, and after witnessing Carroll spend decades telling women to toughen up and stand up for themselves, the through line is obvious. Soon, she was put in a position to practice what she preached.

The trial footage is the draw, but her columns buoy the film. Meeropol shows how a persona built in print and on camera became the thing the defense used against her: She was too loud, too funny, too much for a victim. But Carroll refused to tone it down. Ask E. Jean is a conventional portrait but a compelling one, because the subject—now in her 80s—never flinches or asks to be liked.

The Boys and the Bees is one of this year’s short-film triumphs. In it, we meet Eliza and Nehemiah Ray and their two young sons, Carver and Aaro, living on 12 acres in rural Georgia. We witness the parents’ patience and care for their boys, their bees, and the land that sustains them.

One moment captures the film’s beauty. Carver, the only one in the family yet to be stung by a bee, wants to know what his parents and brother have felt. Nehemiah looks him in the eye and tells him the truth: it’s going to hurt. Carver screams and cries, and his father stays close as it burns, pulling out the stinger. By the end, with his father beside him, Carver is proud of himself.

It’s every lesson at once. To tell the truth, even when it’s hard. To let yourself be pushed but also held. Few films this year say so much in so little time.

Luis Valdez picked crops as a kid growing up in California. Then, in 1965, he founded El Teatro Campesino and staged plays on flatbed trucks for striking grape pickers, who agitated for the first union contracts for farmworkers. Zoot Suit , the play he wrote and directed about the 1943 Los Angeles riots, became the first Chicano production on Broadway, though the critics dismissed it. Valdez went on to make the Ritchie Valens biopic La Bamba , which became one of the biggest hits of 1987. This film tells that story in order, and the order is the argument. Each time Valdez faced rejection, he adapted—eventually landing himself on bigger stages. It is a standard talking-heads tribute, but the archival footage of performances alone is worth the watch.

My last pick is the charming New York Times op-doc Stalin Boys , in which four West Texas middle schoolers write and perform a play about Stalin’s purges to compete in the Texas State History Fair. A middle school boy named Malachi is obsessed with one of the most ruthless dictators the world has ever known; this surely raises eyebrows at school. But his interest is rooted not in admiration but in a healthy curiosity about humanity’s rawest edges.

At one point, Malachi describes Stalin’s father as a drunk who turned cruel. Then, quietly, he mentions his own father, also a drinker, whom he and his mother escaped when they came to Marathon, Texas.

Malachi’s fascination with such dark material is bound up with his own helplessness. Yet the film offers hope at a time when the AI-induced atrophy of young minds and the general outsourcing of curiosity looms so large. We get to smile when we see him practicing his Russian accent with YouTube videos. We see the little boy feel powerful donning a Soviet uniform with dangling medals. More adults, not just middle schoolers in a dwindling railroad town in the high desert of West Texas, should be asking questions like, “So, why’d he turn out like that?”
